answer: Three objects chain together. pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> carries the actual limit on one instance: add/set it with low-threshold and high-threshold (uint64/int64/decimal64, or na / not-supported; default na). direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). show pm-parameter identifies the parameter name and its type (counter or gauge) and units (seconds for errored seconds). pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> must have tca-supervision true (and data-supervision true) for the crossing to be supervised and reported; it also lists supported-parameters, max 100 elements. Type-wide values come from pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>, which shows default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200.

Enable both protocol and authentication: set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true (ntp-enabled defaults true, ntp-auth-enabled defaults false; assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both, default both). Add the key with add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]: key-id range 1..65534, key-type sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value string length 8..40, is-trusted default false. Bind it to the server: add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id> (IPv4, IPv6 or DNS name; origin manual or dhcp, default manual; auth-key-id default not-applicable; admin-state lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock). Check it with show ntp ntp-active-server and show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>: auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means all recent probes answered), stratum, offset, jitter, delay and condition. show clock time-source should read ntp.

protection-switch is the traffic command for a protection group: protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>, with operation-type force, lockout, manual or release. switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. Operational mode only. The same intent can be held on the group itself via set protection-group-<name> pg-request (clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise; default clear), and protection-unit shows state active/standby/available and role working/protection. manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID> moves the controller card, e.g. manual-switchover card-1-3, which prompts: Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is, when NTP is not enabled; that is why the manual set is rejected. Run show clock and read time-source (ntp or manual, default manual), current-time, universal-time, timezone, DST-active, uptime and last-time-jump (jumps of less than 10 seconds are ignored). If time-source is ntp the clock is coming from a server, so check show ntp (ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server, assignment-method manual/dhcp/both) and show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for stratum, offset, delay, jitter, reach (377 means all recent probes answered), auth-status and condition. To set the time by hand, disable NTP first, then use the ISO 8601 form: set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z, or a non-UTC offset such as set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00. The zone is set separately with set clock timezone <value>.

show ne gives the identity: ne-id, ne-name (default 1830 GX), ne-type (G30, G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-site, ne-location, clli, contact, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1) and recover-mode. show equipment (e.g. show equipment card-1-1) lists what is fitted with required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw and last-reboot-reason; show slot compares supported-type with installed-type per position, and show inventory adds serial-number, clei, part-number and fw-status. For the cost of the reboot: restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] restarts the active controller card if no resource is given and does a warm start if no type is given, and it asks for confirmation unless -f. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, connectivity returns within five minutes; warm reboots only the processor and is non service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Not all cards support all restart types.

The equipment holder is slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>, e.g. slot-1-2, showing supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The card in it is card-<name>, created with add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>. Hanging off the card in the AID scheme: port-<card-name>-<port-name>, sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name>, led-<location>/<name>, console-<name>, usb-<card-name>-<port-name> and serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name>. The pluggable itself is tom-<card-name>-<port-name>; adding a TOM auto-creates the tributary port termination point and deleting the TOM deletes it. Read the pluggable FRU data with show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>, for example show inventory-1-3-1: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class and fw-status.

For what the model can do, use show supported-card-<card-type>, e.g. show supported-card-CHM1R. It reports node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw in Watts, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate; default no), default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band) and supported-features. Companions are supported-slot-<card-type>/<slot-name>, supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>, supported-tom and supported-chassis. For the card actually fitted, use show card-<name> (required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, power-profile, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state) and show capabilities-<name>.

The chain must exist bottom-up. add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version ospfv2|ospfv3, default ospfv2] [router-id-mode manual|use-loopback, default use-loopback]; the stated pre-condition is that with router-id-mode use-loopback an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. Then add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>, whose pre-condition is that the OSPF instance must be created first (ospf-area-type normal). Then add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>, whose pre-condition is that both the instance and the area must be present; ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface. Check enable (default true), hello-interval (1..32767, default 10), router-dead-interval (4..65535, default 40), ospf-cost (1..65535, default 10), priority (0..255, default 1) and the ospf-auth-enable/ospf-auth-algorithm/ospf-auth-key trio. Progress is in show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area>/<if-name>/<router-id>: state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, with role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. An OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state> where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, e.g. show software-load-1-5/active or show software-load-active for the whole system. It returns swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-information, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. The individual pieces are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> with state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown), version and description, and beneath it show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>. Firmware bundled with the load is show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version, and versions of the same firmware can differ per equipment-type. Use show current-fw to compare against what the hardware is actually running, and show controller-card for which controller is active or standby.

The per-port control is lldp-admin-status on the comm-eth or ethernet facility: tx-only (transmits but does not store remote system info), rx-only (receives but does not transmit), tx-and-rx, or disabled, with default disabled. So set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx if both directions are needed. Then show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress (the egress direction is not supported): total-frames-out tells you whether you are sending, total-frames-in whether you are receiving, plus total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs, total-ageouts, last-change-time and last-clear-time, all defaulting to 0. All counters for a port freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled on that port. show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> shows what you advertise (chassis-id, port-id, system-name); show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress shows the far end with age and ttl. The global fallback lifetime is set lldp hold-on-timer, default 900 seconds.

show slot lists every position as slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> with supported-type, installed-type (blank when nothing is fitted), oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; avail-state values include equipment-not-present and equipment-mismatch. For the FRU detail of whatever is in a position use show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable; default not-applicable). The running firmware level is show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>, giving fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable), for example show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1. Hardware detected but not yet accepted is under show unprovisioned-inventory.

After download swimage <source>, show manifest lists the downloaded manifest files and show manifest-<manifest-file> gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and information. Contents are shown by show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name>, which returns state, version and description; state is exactly what tells you whether each piece got installed, with values installed, not-installed, installation-failed and unknown (default unknown). Firmware carried in the package is show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version. show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> lists the image files that came down, and show downloads lists the downloads. Once the package becomes a software load the same detail appears under show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> and show sw-subcomponent, with show upgrade-status-<resource> reporting installation status per resource.

Both defaults are type-level profile objects that the system manages and that cannot be manually deleted. Alarm severity: alarm-severity-profile is the container (set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>), and alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> is the individual entry, severity values critical, event, major, minor, not-reported, warning, with direction na/ingress/egress and location na/near-end/far-end; it also shows service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Example: set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major. Performance monitoring: pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> holds default-data-supervision and default-tca-supervision (true/false), which decide whether newly created resources of that type get PM data supervision and threshold crossing supervision enabled automatically. pm-profile global-data-supervision (auto-enabled or manual, default manual) can enable data supervision globally instead, and pm-threshold-profile carries default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold.

ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> makes the decision: action indicates the IPsec treatment given to the IP datagrams and is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. priority (uint8) gives precedence between SPD entries. Its other attributes are ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel or transport (default tunnel), esn default true, anti-replay-window range 32..1024 default 64, and dynamic-ts enabled/disabled default disabled. Underneath the SPD entry hangs ipsec-traffic-selector-<...>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0..255; default any), and under each traffic selector hang local-subnet and remote-subnet (keyed by prefix) and local-ports and remote-ports (keyed by /<start>/<stop>). Also under the SPD entry are ipsec-sa-proposal, encryption-algorithm and ipsec-sa-re-key. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

trusted-certificate-<id> is the CA you trust: the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. local-certificate-<id> is this node's own identity, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; it exposes used-by (secure-applications, ikev2-peers using it), self-signed and subject-alternative-names. peer-certificate-<id> is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, with white-listed true when it was imported with no associated trust chain. All three are set-only for revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control (default allowed) and label, and all show version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length (rsa2048..ecdsa521), key-usage and certificate-bytes in PEM. The fourth, certificate, is the container command: show certificates, show certificate-revocation and clear certificate.

Two routes in. import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>] pastes PEM straight in for trusted-certificate, local-certificate or peer-certificate; -i also imports intermediates present in a bundle, root certificates must be installed individually, and with no certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix (trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, -2). Or fetch from a server: download filetype=<local-certificate|peer-certificate|trusted-certificate|crl> source=scp://user@host/path certificate-name=<name> [passphrase=...], accepting PKCS#12 or PKCS#7. csr-gen creates a signing request, cert-gen a self-signed certificate. Removal: clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<id>, where the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type (use tab to list them); bulk values are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. It prompts Are you sure? [y/n] unless -f is given.

Packet traffic is acl and ace. acl-<name> is the list bound to an interface: add acl-<name> type <IPv4|IPv6> interface <1-AUX-1|1-AUX-2|DCN|DCN-B|DCN-2|DCN-2-B>. ace-<name>/<sequence-id> is the entry that decides whether traffic is permitted: action drop, accept or reject, default drop, matching on source-ip-address, destination-ip-address, L4 lower/upper ports, ttl (1..255, default 255), protocol (default any) and direction (input or output, default input). An ACL must exist before an ACE can be added, and at least one of source IP, destination IP, L4 ports, TTL or protocol must be given. The evaluation order is the ace sequence-id, range 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B and 1-256 for DCN-A, recommended in multiples of 5 so rules can be inserted. show access-control-list simply displays the list. access-rule and access-rule-list have nothing to do with packet traffic: they are management authorization, permitting or denying create/read/update/delete/execute on YANG paths, modules and attributes per user-group.

Rules are processed in the order given by sequence-id and lower number ids are processed first, so the rule with the lower sequence-id takes effect. If sequence-id is not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, meaning the rule goes to the end of the list; ids can be changed over the life of the list to re-sort entries. The access-rule-list itself also carries a sequence-id, ordering the lists against each other. On access-rule-list, user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names, or the default value '*' meaning match all existing user-groups, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. Each access-rule's action, permit or deny, is mandatory whenever a rule is created. For packet filtering the equivalent ordering key is the ace sequence-id within an ACL.

The trap community string is not on snmp-community: the guide states that the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. snmp-community-<name> only carries community-string (length 1..32), enabled (true/false, default true) and community-string-access, which can only be read-only. Set the trap string with add snmp-target-<target-name> ... trap-community-string <value> or set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>; it is a string of length 0..32 and its default value is infinera, which is why a receiver expecting something else rejects the traps. The rest of add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value>: snmp-version v2c or v3 (default v2c), target-port 0..65535 (default 162), target-transport udp, enabled default true. snmpv3-user only applies when snmp-version is v3.

external-fiber-connection is the one written by something other than you: it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, keyed by name with src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, fiber-connection-type (one-way or two-way, default two-way) and scope (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose; if scope is not cable-id, CableID verification does not include the connection). fiber-connection-<name> is the one you configure by hand: the physical link between two distinct ports or sub-ports within the same NE, with src-port, dst-port, label and fiber-connection-type. supporting-fiber-connection-<name> is read-only and just shows the fiber-connection-list supporting an entity. Discovered neighbour data can be cleared with clear topology.

To address the node use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, for example add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0; origin shows static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) or 224 through 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. The other two are read-only LLDP views and configure nothing: management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> retrieves the management address advertised by the remote system on that port and direction, with if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid; management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> is the same data for the addresses this node advertises locally and has no direction key. Each management address must have a distinct address-subtype and address.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method, which is static or dhcp with default static, and set it back with set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static before adding the address. Also confirm ipv4-enabled is true (default true) and admin-state is unlock. The address itself can also be refused: addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or with 224 through 255 are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are allowed to be configured. To see which interfaces are available, type ? after ipv4-address- and the system displays the object completion options; show interface also lists each interface with if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, backup-port, vrf, protection-mode and oper-state.

show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> shows the list of system routes from all sources, including dynamic protocols; source-protocol identifies where each came from (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop is none, blackhole or unreachable, default none. show rib-<rib-name> lists the RIBs, with one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family per routing instance, showing vrf and address-family (ipv4-unicast, ipv6-unicast); all routes in a RIB share one address family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> gives next hops and show routing gives the overall routing view. Hand-entered routes are added with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [distance 1..255, default 1] [interface <value>] [advertised true|false, default false] [origin manual|dhcp, default manual] [special-next-hop blackhole], with ipv6-static-route the IPv6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the IPsec/IKEv2 security tunnel. Both are keyed <ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, so they sit under an ipsec-traffic-selector inside an ipsec-spd-entry: local-ports is the local L4 port range of the selector, remote-ports the far end's. start may be all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0 and the value 0 is only accepted when start is set to all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 and add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. connection-ports is the connectivity object: show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name] returns the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card for a ROADM degree, so that the OMS of the corresponding dwdm port is created. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index is 1..2 but is always 1 in 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>] makes the copy, storing the current configuration database into a backup slot. db-instance is temp (default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage for important configurations), or the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek, plus rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup into chassis storage; description is 0..128 characters. It is refused if the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is not configured, either globally under security-policies or inline on this command; the passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must contain no dictionary words, and uses the 85-character Z85 set. Taking oneweek again overwrites the existing file. activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override true|false, default false] puts it back, with the pre-condition that a snapshot must have been taken. show database lists them (active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp) with database-state, backup-time and description.

activate is one Operational-mode command with several targets: activate-file; swimage (activates the currently installable image, implies a system restart; db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback, default auto); database (activates the currently inactive database, restart-type cold|warm default cold, sanity-check-override false|true default false, checks NE name, shelf serial number and software version); location-led (target chassis or card, led-mode flash|solid default flash, timeout 0..120 s default 0 meaning no timeout); eqpt-fw (resource plus fw-image-name); krp (installs a key replacement package); otdr and otdr-fiber-check; loopback (WSS loopback on an NMC). Unless -f is given the user must confirm. For database snapshots there is a separate command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>], with the pre-condition that a snapshot was taken (take-snapshot).

show capabilities-<name> is the per-card one: name is the card name and it retrieves that card's capabilities. show l0-capabilities is the photonic one: it takes no parameters and shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions. show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs] is the add/drop one: max-degrees is the maximum number of degrees (20, uint8; 0 if not supported, degrees exist only on OADM node types, ILA is 0 by convention because it has two fixed directions) and max-adgs is the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (110, uint8; also OADM-only). Note that max-degrees is the maximum working degree-number, not necessarily the supported deployment configuration. All three are show-only and run in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

show controller-card-<name> displays only the controller: redundancy-status active|standby|not-in-service (default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status ready-synchronized|not-ready-synchronizing|not-ready-synchronize-fail|lock-out|card-not-present (default not-ready-synchronizing), number-of-switchover-events and time-of-last-switchover (both visible only on the active controller), and additional-details (string 0..128). show card-<name> is the card-base object common to all card types: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name/slot-name/subslot-name, power-profile, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, admin-state lock|maintenance|unlock (default unlock), oper-state, avail-state. show supported-card-<card-type> is the per-model capability table: supported-subtype, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands, supported-features.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec object: add macsec-entity-<name> supporting-facility (for example ethernet-6-3-3), enabled default true, link-security-control must-secure|should-secure (default must-secure), replay-protection enable|disable, replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 (default 0). Its cipher is not configured here; it is read back as negotiated-cipher-suite and chosen through mka-policy macsec-cipher-suite. secure-entity is the optical/L1 encryption object: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility (optical-carrier, odu or OTUflex) plus remote-secure-entity, enabled default false, re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic|continue-traffic (default continue-traffic), traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0). Its cipher terms live in the read-only secure-entity-sa-proposal: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521.

ase-idler-service is the ASE idler filling function on a card (add/delete/set/show): ase-idler-enable enabled|disabled, default disabled, turns ASE filling on the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum; ase-idler-state reports ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted or ase-disabled (default ase-disabled); function is idler; alarm-report-control default allowed. ase-idler-source is the ASE pump that produces the signal (set/show only): pump-enable enabled|disabled default disabled, pump-state, target-output-power range -3.00..20.50 dBm default 13, admin-state lock|unlock|maintenance default unlock, function ase-idler-source, with supporting-input-port and supporting-output-port. sw-service does not belong with them: show sw-service-<sv-name> or show sw-services lists the software services and containers on the node, with state off|ok|fail, state-details, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No, they are not harmless. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<enabled|disabled> toggles Zero Touch Provisioning: change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot; change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops it if it is already running. Current mode is read with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, which confirms the current configuration as-is, re-enables communication with the line cards and potentially reconfigures traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting; it has no parameters. Both are Operational mode and prompt for confirmation unless -f is given. The carrier-mode commands are read-only by comparison: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> and show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> only display capacity, client-mode, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status and supported-subtypes.

State: show third-party-app-<app-name> gives state running|stopped|failed (default stopped) and enable true|false (default false; when enabled the app is started, including after a system restart), plus version, vendor, product and information; show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> gives version, state and information per location. Firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> gives file-status valid|invalid|missing, path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version, present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt (max 80 elements each). Clearing: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value> clears third party apps. To act on a stuck app without clearing it, use appctl [app-name=] [command=]restart|netls|exec [[target=]] [[parameters=]]; target defaults to system, and parameters apply to restart or exec (max 50 elements).

Per-session is cli-session-config: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value> where cli-lines is the number of rows before pausing, range 10..1000, default 40; also cli-columns 80..4000 default 80, interactive-mode true|false default true (set per CLI session and not persistent), and display-timestamp default false. The protocol as a whole is cli: enabled default true (it cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port 1..65535 default 22, script-dir, default-interactive-mode default true (affects only newly created sessions), and show-alarm-columns default default-columns, which has global effect on all CLI sessions. The two system configuration objects are config (show config [<entity-id>|<entity-type>], displays non-default configuration recursively from the current scope) and extended-config (add/delete/show extended-config-<name>, a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behaviour globally; the name must match one known by the system).

set is the generic attribute assignment: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...], at least one attribute-value pair, all belonging to the same managed entity; it supports wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), ranges card-1-[1..4] and lists, and asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances. set-alarm-state is a separate operation: set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>...) changes the operator state of alarms, with states none, ack and close, from 1 up to 10 alarm-ids, and acknowledge-text 0..256 characters. set-time [new-time=]<value> changes the system time and is only applicable when the time-source is manual (NTP not enabled), using ISO 8601 form 2017-01-12T10:22:25Z or an offset such as +03:00. The one ending in -set is unrelated: named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> value <string 1..1024>.

mc is the Media Channel, a spectrum slot on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value> in MHz; center-frequency and slot-width (upper minus lower) are computed by the system; auto-delete default disabled; the referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. nmc is the Network Media Channel, the per-carrier channel whose parent-facility can be a Media Channel or an OMS: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <190650000..196700000 MHz> [width 15000..200000 MHz, default 35000, configured as the 3 dB bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate], plus power, attenuation and ASE-insertion attributes. The fillers occupy unused spectrum and are system-created: mc-f is show-only (lower-frequency, upper-frequency, slot-width) and nmc-f is show plus set of admin-state and alarm-report-control, reporting alloc- and actual- lower/upper-frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz) and power-actual-tx/rx.

The scan is run by activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>], or activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> for a manual OTDR-based fiber check (up to 3 tests; it returns an error if a manual scan or automatic Raman fiber check is already in progress). Tuning lives in otdr-ptp: otdr-range auto or 0..300.0 km (set it to fiber length plus 10 percent), otdr-pulse-width auto or 10..20000 ns, otdr-measurement-speed fast|medium|slow|precision|auto|high-precision, otdr-ior auto or 1.0..2.0, otdr-fiber-type (auto, SSMF, SMF-ULL, LEAF and others), otdr-resolution auto or 0.4..100.0, peak-power auto or 5..14.5, launching-fiber-length 0..50 m (default 0, auto not supported). The answer comes out of otdr-ptp: otdr-fiber-break-distance in km, or not-available if no break was identified, plus otdr-last-measurement and the generated .sor file in otdr-last-measurement-file. Progress is in otdr: otdr-state not-available|idle|measuring|finished|fail, otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-port, otdr-measurement-direction and otdr-error.

Each dns-server entry carries origin: dhcp means the address was assigned to the system by a DHCP server, manual means it was configured by hand (default manual). An entry that keeps coming back after deletion is being re-supplied by DHCP; convert it with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Whether DHCP values are taken at all is decided by dns assignment-method manual|dhcp|both, default both, alongside dns enabled true|false (default true) and dns search (suffix, must contain at least one dot, 0..64). For the relay there are two levels: the global dhcp-relay with mode disabled|ipv4|ipv6 (default disabled) and server-address (at least one IP must be configured when enabled), and the per-interface if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true|false, default false, which enables the function on that interface and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay that does nothing is usually mode disabled or dhcp-relay-enabled still false.

clear [-f] system [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] does the secure wipe, with three types. factory-reset resets the system or a specific chassis/card to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations; it does not take effect for G30 OCC2T/OCC2E but is supported for the G30 FRCU controller. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software, and recovery then requires a base software reinstall from ONIE. inactive only clears the inactive software partition. target defaults to the whole system; restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown, and shutdown is not supported on the L0 cards. If you want to keep logs and PM data, use clear [-f] database instead (clear-type full, keep-networking or initialize-from-script): it resets the database and reboots, and the guide states it does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data.

show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name> lists inventory that has been detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration; it reports actual-type, actual-subtype, hardware-version, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp, the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> shows the NCT links the system filled in dynamically, with src-chassis, dst-chassis and src-chassis-state/dst-chassis-state of node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned; ports on an unprovisioned chassis appear as <chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>. Once the shelf is added, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller, chassis-role unknown|main-chassis|sub-chassis, expected-serial-number (which informs the NC of a sub-chassis serial number) and equipment-discovery-ready, which stays false until all equipment was discovered at startup.

The deciding attribute is amplifier control-mode: auto-max-pw (default), where the system sets the gain automatically targeting maximum output power, or manual, where you set gain-target yourself in the range 0..40 dB (default 0.0). amp-control-support tells you whether auto is even possible on that card: auto means both manual and auto-max-pw are supported, manual-only means only manual. gain-range-control follows control-mode automatically (manual with manual, auto with auto-max-pw), with gain-range-target standard|low|high; in auto mode use gain-adjustment [-20.00..20.00] dB, supported only where function is pa or inline. Nothing comes out if amplifier-enable is disabled (the default), if forced-shutdown is true, if admin-state is lock, or after an input OLOS shutdown once olos-shutdown-soak-timer (0..2000 ms) expires, unless olos-shutdown-disable is true. Output also depends on the OSC signal for node-type ILA, or on the OMS facilities and an OXcon for node-type OADM. Read back gain-operating, pump-state, output-power-mon and control-state.

show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> tells you which member is live: state is active, standby, available or unknown, with role working or protection and transport-entity giving the underlying facility. At group level, show protection-group-<name> pg-state reports no-request, forced-to-working/protection, manual-to-working/protection, sf-on-working, sd-on-protection, wait-to-restore, protection-lockout, frozen and so on (default unavailable), plus last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. Switch behaviour is configured on protection-group: switching-mode unidirectional (default) or bidirectional, reversion-mode revertive|non-revertive (default non-revertive), hold-off-timer 0..10000 ms in 1 ms steps (default 0), wtr-timer 60..720 s (default 300, revertive only), and the triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, all disabled by default. Operate it with protection-switch [-f] operation-type=force|lockout|manual|release switch-target= protection-group=, or set pg-request.

Trigger it with verify [-f] fiber-connection [target-select=]<port-id> [allow-switching]; if the port-id is omitted, all paths are verified, and if the port takes part in several CableID paths, all of them are included. allow-switching is false by default, which checks active paths only; true lets the system initiate OPSM switching so working and protection paths are both verified. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. On acceptance the NE raises CID-verification-in-progress and the command returns immediately. Watch it with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state idle|running-incl-switching|running-no-switching and test-progress as N out of M completed. Results per port pair are in show [-r] cable-id-path-<name>: card-type-a/port-a and card-type-z/port-z (CAD10A or RD20TM), port-a-to-port-z-last-test-status and the reverse, not-verified|pass|fail, the path-status fields, last-test-qualifier up-to-date|out-dated, last-test-timestamp and additional-info (Cable-ID-MISMATCH, Cable-ID TxLOS, Cable-ID RxLOS, Cable-ID-RxLOF, power out-of-range, timeout). terminate cable-id stops running tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by security-policies aaa-authentication-method: local-only (the default, in which case the node never contacts RADIUS at all), local-first-then-remote, remote-first-then-local, or remote-unavailable-then-local. Authorization has its own policy, aaa-authorization-method, also local-only by default; changing it requires the user to log out and back in. The target itself is aaa-server-<server-name>: protocol-supported RADIUS (default) or TACACSPLUS, server-address, server-priority 1-10 (lowest number is highest precedence), enabled default true, shared-secret default sharedkey with a 64 character maximum, server-port-authentication default 1812, server-port-accounting default 1813, server-port default 49, source-ip and role-supported authentication/authorization/accounting. What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, 1..90 seconds default 5, and retry, 0..5 with a default of 3; total wait, timeout x (retry + 1), should stay under 5 minutes. TACACS+ counters are visible with show aaa-statistics.

The automation account's public key goes in ssh-authorized-key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]. Each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication, for a local or remote user; user-name 0..32, key-id 1..64, public-key up to 2048 characters in OpenSSH/PEM form, with public-key-algorithm ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 or ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096. Also set security-policies ssh-authentication-method to public-key or public-key-or-password, since the default is password. The remote host the node copies files to goes in ssh-known-host: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <hostname/IPv4/IPv6> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value>, which additionally accepts ssh-ed25519 (from R9.0). How strictly that identity is enforced is security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking, strict or relaxed (default relaxed). The node's own keys are separate: show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> lists the global host keys (one per algorithm, auto-generated in the default DB), and ssh-keygen [-b=<len>] [-t=rsa|ecdsa|ed25519] [-l=<label>] regenerates them.

The key agreement policy is mka-policy, referenced by the macsec entity of the Ethernet facility: add/set mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority] [macsec-cipher-suite] [confidentiality-offset] [sak-rekey-interval]. key-server-priority is what MKA uses to elect the key server, macsec-cipher-suite is the cipher suite for Secure Association Key derivation, and confidentiality-offset is the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain text. The session key rollover is sak-rekey-interval, the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. The policy is bound per port through macsec-mka-<name> mka-policy <name>, which also holds connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (0..64), psk-lifetime 1..173 days (default 14), psk-expiration-warning, psk-lifetime-enable, and reports is-key-server. Watch the channels with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>: sci-tx or sci-rx as a 16 character hex string, state in-use or not-in-use, association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number.

netconf: enabled true by default and it cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session; port is the SSH listening port, range 1..65535, default 830; hello-timeout 1..3600 seconds, default 2; annotate-cli-name false; static-info-in-notifs up to 10 YANG identifiers. grpc, which carries gNMI: enabled true by default, port default 50051, gnmi-get-encoding-granularity per-path or per-object with per-object as the default. restconf: enabled true by default and https-enabled true with https-port 1..65535 default 8181, but http-enabled is false out of the box (RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode) with http-port default 8080, and cookie-timeout 1..300 minutes default 5. So the only thing off by default is RESTCONF over plain HTTP. For comparison the CLI protocol itself listens over ssh on cli port 22 with enabled true.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] defaults to a warm restart if type is not given, and restarts the active node controller card if no resource-id is given. warm reboots the processor of the card (CHM6, UCM4 and similar) and is non service affecting, with connectivity back within five minutes, though on XMM4 visibility is lost for about 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, again with connectivity regained within five minutes, but a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting and only loses visibility. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. No, you cannot assume uniform behaviour: the guide states explicitly that not all cards support all restart types. Restartable entities are card (cold, warm, shutdown), a card sub-component (cold, warm; list them with show card resources) and tom (cold only). The command asks for confirmation unless -f is supplied.

Three things. First a template per TOM part-number: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>], where ports-applicable is all by default, or up to 20 named ports such as T1 or T10. Second the parameter values inside it: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<entry-name> value <value>, for example RxAmplitude, RxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQ, TxEQAdaptive. Third the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true, which is disabled by default; on enabling, templates are not applied retroactively, only from that moment onward. Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes (see supported-card support-serdes-config). When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically; swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Manual serdes settings are kept even where they deviate from the template, and apply-template forces re-application.

ots, the Optical Transport Section, is the fiber span: fiber-type-tx/rx, fiber-length-tx/rx, span-loss-reference with span-loss-transmit/receive and span-loss-derived values, external-attenuation-tx/rx, raman-coefficient-tx/rx, target-power-setting, loading-policy, osc-less (default disabled, for interworking with systems having no compatible OSC or spans outside the OSC budget) and the read-only laser-safety-mode, OPLM (Optical Power Limited Mode, default) or APSD (Automatic Power Shut Down). oms, the Optical Multiplex Section, is the multiplexed spectrum: band-allowed/band-actual/band-target, grid-mode (flexible, fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-100G-48ch and others), configured-spectrum, target-output-power, attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx; MCs and NMCs hang off it. ops, the Optical Physical Section, is the port-level section carrying role tributary, multi-carrier, active-multi-carrier, general-purpose or ase-input, plus input-psd-profile and port-expansion no|y-cable. osc, the Optical Supervisory Channel, carries the supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE with FEC (HSC OLS only), osc-wavelength, l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6, osc-control auto|manual.

That behaviour is trib-ptp tributary-disable-action, which defines what the NE does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed. The default is laser-shut-off; the other values are none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). Delay it with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 which disables the hold-off; the guide notes this timer applies when the TDA action is laser turn-off, so the optical signal is held until the timer expires before the laser is turned off. Related switches on the same object: near-end-tda enabled|disabled (default disabled), tda-degrade-mode enabled|disabled (default disabled, BERSD-ODU triggering ALS) and forward-defect-trigger true|false (default true), which decides whether a received client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

The high-order ODU appears on its own: 'The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created' - use 'show odu' to confirm it exists. Low-order ODUs you add by hand: 'add odu-<name> odu-type <value> parent-odu <HO-ODU> [time-slots|opucn-time-slots] [trib-port-number]'. The stated pre-condition is 'Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added'. odu-type: ODUCn, ODUCni, ODU4, ODU4i, ODUflexi, ODUflex, ODU0, ODU1, ODU2, ODU2e. The 'class' attribute is set by the system from creation order - high-order for the topmost system-created ODUCn/ODUk, low-order (default) for the children. OTUs are added manually too, e.g. 'add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1'. Every facility shows managed-by (system or user, default system); only user-created facilities can be user deleted.

The BERT is the 'bert' command (Operational mode): 'bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10', plus bert stop/get/delete (test-id mandatory for stop). test-signal-type: none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV, scrambled-idles; monitoring type adds fec-frames. test-duration 0 (default) means indefinite, min 10 seconds, max 1000 hours. The test pattern is injected on odu-diagnostics: 'set odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> test-signal-type <none|PRBS31Q|PRBS13Q|scrambled-idles|PRBS9|PRBS31|PRBS31NONINV>' (default none), test-signal-direction ingress/egress/both (default ingress), test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loopback is the 'loopback' attribute on otu, odu and optical-carrier: none (default), facility or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

A secure-entity must exist at each end, bound to its local facility and pointed at the far end: 'add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <value> [enabled true]'. supporting-facility is the local facility (optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 on 1830 GX G40, odu-1-3-2-ODU4-1 on 1830 GX G30). remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier (G40), the remote ODU (G30), or the remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption, and is settable only on add. enabled defaults to false, so it has to be set true; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited. re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic), traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0, applies only with kill-traffic). 'show data-path-encryption' displays the datapath encryption attributes.

The 'telemetry' command configures the two kinds, persistent and dynamic telemetry ('show telemetry', 'set telemetry id <string>', length 0..4096); the object is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. 'show subscriptions' lists subscriptions. 'show current-subscription-<subscription-name>' shows what is configured now: related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false). What each one watches comes from 'show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<path-name>': subscription-path, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval ms (default 0; a target-defined stream is auto-adjusted to 10 s), heartbeat-interval ms (default 0; auto-adjusted to 20 s), suppress-redundant (default true).

'show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]' shows the protection at rest: encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup / failed-on-bootup / disabled, mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity (changed via the db-migrate RPC). Before a copy the db-passphrase must be configured - the system only accepts 'take-snapshot' if it is set globally with 'set security-policies db-passphrase' or given locally as 'take-snapshot db-passphrase=***'. It needs a minimum of 40 characters (policy range 40..200), no dictionary words, Z85 85-character set; automatic snapshots stay disabled until it is set. 'take-snapshot [db-passphrase=] [db-instance=] [description=]' stores to db-backup (default) or system-backup, db-instance temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek, rollback. List with 'show database'.

Check the configured route first: 'show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf> [advertised] [next-hop-address] [distance] [interface] [monitoring-state] [monitoring-instance] [special-next-hop]' - distance 1..255 (default 1), advertised default false, monitoring-state unmonitored/ok/failed, and the VRF bound to the interface must match the vrf given on the static route. Then 'show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]': special-next-hop none (default), blackhole or unreachable tells you it is deliberately not forwarding. 'show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> next-hop-address' gives the resolved hop. For the instance, 'show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]' shows which VRF that RIB is bound to and whether it is ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; each routing instance gets one system-controlled default RIB per address family. 'show vrf-<name> type' reports mgmt or internal.

'show security-policies' holds the password rules: strict-password-check (default true) requires minimum length 8, one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number, one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; minimum-password-length 1..200 (default 8); enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of the previous 5 passwords, password-history-size 1..200 (default 5). These only affect newly defined passwords. Lockout is per user: 'show user-<name>' gives user-status (enabled, disabled, password-aged, lockout), failed-logins, max-invalid-login 0..255 (default 5 consecutive invalid attempts before suspension), suspension-time 0..1440 minutes (default 5), password-aging-interval 0..999 days (default 90). security-policies also has disable-user-lockout. To clear the session: 'show session' for the session-id (<ip-address>:<port>), then 'kill-session <session-id>' - it cannot be your own session.

'show syslog' defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Console logging is off by default (log-console enabled defaults to false). Remote servers default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, enabled true, origin manual, sensitive-data none, source-facilities all. Rotation lives on log-file: number-of-files 1..20, default 10 - when rotating because max size is reached, the oldest files are discarded once the total exceeds it - and max-file-size 1..30 MB, default 30. Severity is informational and above by default and the default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. The single remote switch is 'set syslog remote-logging-switch false': if false, all remote logging destinations are disabled.

'show current-alarms [number-of-alarms] [last-changed]' lists what is raised now, with a count and the timestamp of the last raise or clear; 'show alarms' and 'show alarm-<alarm-id>' give detail (perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, corrective-action, operator-state). Most alarms have automatic raise and clear criteria; a small subset has no clear criteria and must be acknowledged and cleared by hand with 'clear [-f] alarm <alarm-type> [resource=<value>]' in Operational mode. Find that subset with 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'; it applies only to system-wide alarms not associated with a particular resource. Whether inhibiting reporting drops the ones already up is 'set alarm-control arc-behavior': clear-alarms clears current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, leave-alarms (the default) leaves them raised. alarm-control also has alarm-soaking-behavior, automatic (default) or no-soak.

'status equipment' is the dashboard: it summarises chassis, cards per chassis with subtype and TOMs per card, and per equipment gives temperature sensors, power values, presence or absence, oper-state and alarms (for example 'chassis-1 G42 (NC) temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W', 'card-1-1 XMM4 (Act) temp 25C'). Narrow it by passing the chassis id as the filter, e.g. 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is all chassis or exactly one. For per-slot numbers use 'show pm', whose real-time PM reports temperature (C) per card and fan-speed (percent) per FAN with instant, avg, min and max; narrow with 'show pm card-1-7' or -i=<chassis-name>. Physically it is reflected by the LEDs: 'show leds' or 'show led-<location>/<name> status', values not-available, off, green, flashing-green, yellow, amber, red, flashing-red, cycling.

The line is the OTS. 'show ots-<name>' reports span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx - the measured span loss from OSC powers including losses external to the fiber, 0..99 dB, where 99 dB means OLOS and it is only relevant when an OSC channel exists - against the configured span-loss-transmit (0..80 dB, default 0) and span-loss-receive (0..80 plus 99 dB, default 0; changing it is traffic affecting). span-loss-reference picks which is used, measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80, 99 dB, default 99) is set autonomously and persists across reboot; in measured mode force it with 'update'. Also span-loss-aging-margin-rx 0.00..10.00 dB (default 1.0) and external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB (default 0). The amplifier: 'show amplifier-<name>' gives gain-operating and gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual (standard/low/high), input-power-mon and output-power-mon (-99.00..99.00 dBm), tilt-actual, control-state (converged, fine-tuning, adjusting, stopped) and span-loss-control (default enabled; must be enabled when span-loss-reference is measured).

Client to line, the digital (Layer 1) objects are: trib-ptp, the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver and the protocol layer; the client protocol facility ethernet (or otu, fc, stm, eth-zr); the client low-order odu; the xcon joining the ends ('add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1', direction two-way); then the line-side low-order ODU, its parent high-order ODU (ODUCn/ODUCni, system-created with the super-channel), the otu (OTUCn/OTU4) or flexo-group, and line-ptp. The handover to the optical domain is at the line port: super-channel and optical-carrier (frequency, wavelength, tx-power, modulation-format) are Layer 0, tied via oxcon to nmc (parent-facility a Media Channel or an OMS, center-frequency, width), then oms and ots on the fiber. 'show facilities' lists them; supporting-facilities and supported-facilities on each object walk parent to child.

No, they are separate objects. A counter limit is a PM threshold: per instance 'add|set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]'; per resource type 'set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>', e.g. 'set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200'. Values are a number (uint64, int64, decimal64), na or not-supported, default na; whether crossing is reported is gated by tca-supervision on pm-control-entry or default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry. How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>' (e.g. OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor) or 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>'. Severities: critical, event, major, minor, not-reported, warning; 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type> default-severity' gives the system default.

Stop it reporting with alarm-report-control on the object: 'set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited'. Values are allowed (alarm reporting is allowed) and inhibited; on card the default is inhibited, while on facilities (odu, otu, trib-ptp, line-ptp, ots, amplifier, nmc, flexo-group) the default is allowed, so inhibit those individually to quiet the whole slot. You can also set admin-state to maintenance (values lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock). What happens to alarms already raised is decided system-wide by alarm-control: 'set alarm-control arc-behavior clear-alarms' clears the current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms - the default - leaves them raised. Check with 'show alarm-control [arc-behavior] [alarm-soaking-behavior]'.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. 'show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert]': active-certificate-id (string 0..128) is the list of assigned certificates and in-use is a leafref to it, i.e. what is actually presented. Set it with 'set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client', or comma-separated for several, 'set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY'. type is server or client; status enabled or disabled. The certificate must be imported first: 'import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM string> <passphrase>', with the CA chain imported as trusted-certificate (-i also imports intermediates from a bundle; root certificates must be installed individually). Inspect with 'show local-certificate-<id>' (status in-use/unused/revoked/expired/available, valid-from, valid-to, trust-chain, used-by). For mutual TLS set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled).

Pipe the show output through display csv: 'show pm <command flag> | display csv' gives CSV data importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; 'display xml' and 'display json' are also available. Narrow to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter parameters - period pm-15min, plus data-type, parameter, resource, resource-type or AID - and use -t for a single generic table instead of per-resource tables. Time filters are -st=<timestamp> and -et=<timestamp> (format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00), or -sbin= and -ebin= where bin 0 is current data and bins 1 to n are history. -n= caps records per chassis (default 1000), -s= skips entries so data can be fetched in multiple requests, -i=<chassis-name> limits to one chassis (once per command). 'show pm <tab>' lists all supported filters.

Use 'show pm-catalog <string>', where string is the catalog name, e.g. 'show pm-catalog parameter-undersized', which returns the parameter with its units and type (units packets, type counter). The equivalent per-parameter lookup is 'show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]', e.g. 'show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds' or 'show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized'; 'show pm-parameter' with no argument lists all PM parameters. Both commands are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-control, which configures the currently existing resources in the system that support PM data: 'set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false', e.g. 'set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false'. data-supervision is real-time data supervision for that resource, values true or false, default true. 'show pm-control' displays the current configuration. The equivalent per-instance attribute is on pm-resource: 'set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false' (true/false, default true), readable with 'show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision'. Both work in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes - pm-control-entry is keyed exactly that way, one resource, one period, one direction, one location: 'set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [data-supervision <value>] [tca-supervision <value>]', so 'set pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true' enables threshold-crossing supervision for only that combination. direction takes ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location takes all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h. data-supervision and tca-supervision are true or false. 'show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [supported-parameters] [data-supervision] [tca-supervision]' also lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, maximum 100 elements. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]'. type states the type of PM parameter, either counter or gauge. units reports one of: na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. Example: 'show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized' returns units packets, type counter. 'show pm-parameter' alone lists the available parameters, and 'show pm-catalog <name>' returns the same two fields. Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, on the pm-profile object: 'set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled'. That parameter exists specifically to globally enable PM data-supervision without having to toggle it individually. Values are auto-enabled (global enabling of the PM data-supervision flag) and manual, with manual as the default, meaning the flag is instead controlled per resource type via pm-profile-entry or directly per resource via pm-control-entry. The pm-profile contains information on all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Read it with 'show pm-profile'. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-profile-entry, the PM configuration per resource type: 'set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision <value>] [default-tca-supervision <value>]'. default-data-supervision decides, for newly created resources of this type, whether they have PM data supervision automatically enabled; default-tca-supervision does the same for PM threshold crossing supervision. Both are true or false. direction takes ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location takes all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h. Read back with 'show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision] [default-tca-supervision]'. pm-profile global-data-supervision must stay at manual (its default) for pm-profile-entry to be the controlling level.

Use 'show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset', for example 'show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9'. real-time-data-last-reset is the date and time of the last real time data reset for that resource, and if the data was never reset it is the date and time of that resource's creation (type date-and-time). The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string 1..64 characters) and real-time-supervision (true/false, default true), plus the associated pm-control-entry instances. The counters themselves are cleared with 'clear pm real-time', optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, AID, period (pm-15min, pm-24h, pm-real-time), direction (all, egress, ingress) and location (all, far-end, na, near-end).

Use pm-threshold, which is keyed per instance: 'add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]', for example .../pm-15min/ingress/near-end/errored-seconds with high-threshold set. Use 'set pm-threshold-...' to change it, 'show pm-threshold-... [low-threshold] [high-threshold]' to read it, 'delete pm-threshold-...' to remove it. resource is the Instance ID of an existing system resource and parameter is a PM parameter (counter or gauge). direction takes ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location takes all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64, decimal64), na or not-supported, defaulting to na. For a whole resource type instead of one facility, use pm-threshold-profile.

Use pm-threshold-profile, the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type: 'show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]'. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter; min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values for it. All of them, like the configured low-threshold and high-threshold, are a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na (not applicable) or not-supported. Configure with set, e.g. 'set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200'. direction default all; location default all. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the clock command. Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'. The value list runs from International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00]; the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where the node gets its time, read the time-source attribute: 'show clock time-source' returns ntp (the NE uses NTP for synchronization) or manual (the NE uses its own internal clock); the default is manual. 'show clock' also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, which reports '<time1> to <time2>' and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. If DNS is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond.

Yes. 'set ne node-type OADM' converts it. node-type takes ILA, OADM or XPDR; it can only be set/changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA. G31/G32 chassis support only OADM, G42 defaults to XPDR. Beginning with R7.0 the G34c supports OADM node-type. Pre-conditions to configure node-type OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no spectrum (or ochm) objects exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to configure ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA, not with OADM.

'show ne-function' lists the NE generic functions in one place. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The output enumerates the node's directions and amplifier objects together, for example on a 1830 GX G30 node: direction-1 through direction-8, amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and the ne-function entry itself.

Use 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true'. ntp-enabled takes true/false and defaults to true; ntp-auth-enabled takes true/false and defaults to false, so authentication must be turned on explicitly. The ntp object also carries assignment-method (manual, dhcp or both, default both), which selects whether the system uses manually configured values, DHCP-supplied values, or both. 'show ntp [ntp-enabled] [ntp-auth-enabled] [ntp-active-server] [assignment-method]' displays the state, including the currently active NTP server. The ntp object is system-managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Authentication itself needs an ntp-key, referenced from a server via 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>'.

NTP keys are managed with 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]', plus matching set/show/delete forms. key-type, the hash algorithm for NTP message digest computation, accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 and md5; there is no default. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40 characters. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true/false, defaulting to false. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera'.

Yes. The ntp-server origin attribute is exactly for this: a user can convert a DHCP configured NTP entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute. Run 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual'. origin takes dhcp (address assigned to this system by a DHCP server) or manual (address manually configured), and the default is manual. Other ntp-server attributes are auth-key-id (uint32 or not-applicable, default not-applicable), label (0..256 chars), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed); show adds oper-state and avail-state. The ip-address key may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS domain name. At the ntp level, assignment-method (manual, dhcp, both; default both) controls which configured values the system uses.

Use 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>', for example 'show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218'. The reach attribute is the reachability indicator: it is an 8-bit shift register with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position, and a value of 377 means all the recent probes have been answered. Supporting attributes are when (seconds elapsed since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay to the server in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition (for example sys.peer, reject, candidate). Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]' takes type cold, warm or shutdown. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes. A cold reboot of an XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost. warm reboots only the processor of the CHM6, UCM4, etc. and is non service affecting, again regaining connectivity within five minutes; a warm reboot of an XMM4 loses visibility for 3 minutes. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. If you do not give <type>, the default is warm; if you do not give <resource-id>, the active controller card is restarted. Cards support cold/warm/shutdown, card sub-components cold/warm, toms cold only, and not all cards support all types. Confirmation is required unless -f is given.

Because set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. If NTP is running the node takes its time from the server and the manual set is rejected; check with 'show clock time-source' (ntp or manual, default manual) and disable NTP with 'set ntp ntp-enabled false' if you really need to set it by hand. The syntax is 'set-time [new-time=]<value>' in Operational mode, with the value in a format derived from ISO 8601 combining date and time, for example 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z' where Z is UTC. A non-UTC timezone is allowed by supplying +/-hh:mm instead of Z, for example 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Retrieve the current time with the 'time' command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in set-time.

Yes, 'status equipment'. The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details such as temperature sensors and power values, listing chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, and generic status: presence or absence, oper-state and alarms. The default scope is the entire network element. For large NEs you can filter per chassis by giving the chassis id, for example 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. Output uses symbols: a check for oper-state enabled/admin-state unlocked/no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Syntax is 'status [[dashboard=]<system | equipment | L0-oxcon | L0-ocm | L1-traffic>] [[filter=]<value>]', Operational mode.

Use 'clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. type is the mode: factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity; full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the SW on controller and line-cards, and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover; inactive clears the inactive software partition. restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown, where the system does not restart afterwards. target is the whole system or a specific chassis or card AID; with no target the entire system is cleared. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect on 1830 GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported on the G30 controller card (FRCU), and factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. For a simple database wipe use 'clear database'. Example: 'clear system factory-reset shutdown'.

Just type 'time'. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.
