If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole. That applies to both ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route, where special-next-hop takes the value blackhole. Create the advertisement with add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>; instance-id is a string of length 1..255, remote-address is the BGP peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6), and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network managed objects can be configured. Example: add bgp-network-10/2620:38:4001:192::65/3000::2/64

The comm-channel mtu attribute is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when mode is L3. It is an unsigned 16-bit integer with a platform-dependent range: 1280..1500 octets on 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500; for 1830 GX G40 the defaults per interface type are DCN 1518, AUX 1518, AUX2 1518, OFEC-CC 1518, Craft 1518, CHM6 1518 and UCM4 1518. mtu can be given on add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] or changed with set comm-channel-<name> [mtu <value>]. The related mru is a separate uint16 in range 64..1500 octets, default 1500, also only when mode is L3. mode takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3. Example: add comm-channel-gcc0 type GCC0 label GCC0 alarm-report-control allowed mtu 1500 parent otu-1-6-1-OTUC4

LLDP is not on by default. lldp-admin-status on comm-eth defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only, rx-only and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if mode is L1 (mode takes L1, L2 or L3, default L3). lldp-transmit-interval is the interval to transmit LLDP Tx TLVs, an integer in the range 1..16383 seconds, default 30 seconds. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP address is used as the management address; it must be explicitly set and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx, with values 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only) and L0-MGMT. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. rate and duplex-mode are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled: rate takes 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum, and duplex-mode defaults to full. Example: set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx

Use set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], and read it back with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]; both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with default disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses as an IPv4 or IPv6 server address; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3 to do both in one command. This is the global setting. Per-interface enabling is separate: if-dhcp-relay has dhcp-relay-enabled (true or false, default false) which enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure it with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and view it with show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is a true or false flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a String of length 0..64 which must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Individual servers carry their own origin attribute (dhcp or manual) on dns-server. Example: set DNS enabled true

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where the entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one simply by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> [origin <value>]. View it with show dns-server-<address> [origin], and remove an entry with delete dns-server-<address>. All forms run in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. The global dns object controls whether DHCP-supplied servers are accepted at all, through assignment-method (manual, dhcp or both, default both).

Use the if-dhcp-relay command: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>], and check it with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. Both are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a String of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on this interface and takes true or false, with default false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (it defaults to disabled) and at least one server-address should be configured for the relay to do anything. Examples: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled.

By default a new interface is statically addressed and protected. ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user given protection mode, taking unknown, protected or unprotected, and defaults to protected; the read-only protection-state reports the current state and defaults to unknown. Syntax: add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [if-description <value>] [protection-mode <value>] [ipv4-enabled <value>] [ipv4-address-assignment-method <value>] [ipv6-enabled <value>] [ipv6-address-assignment-method <value>] [proxy-arp-enabled <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control to allowed, proxy-arp-enabled to false (DCN interface only). Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and its result takes action on configured static-routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into failed state and takes none or withdraw, with default withdraw, so the route is pulled by default. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, a string with a maximum of 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6 address) and next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address; the instance will not be active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled defaults to true. The static route then shows monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. if-name is the interface object identifier, a String of length 0..64 characters, and netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask; only valid netmasks are allowed to be configured. Read it back with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. The following addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback addresses), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental addresses). origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, defaulting to static. To list the available interfaces, type ? after ipv4-address-. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask 255.255.240.0 and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0

On ipv4-static-route, distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255 with default 1. Create the route with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes are needed because routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in the IGP tables you configure blackhole static routes. Other attributes: advertised is true or false, default false, and when set the route is advertised in the routing protocol, for OSPF as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual; interface must be bound to the same VRF as the static-route vrf. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165

It is the same pattern but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is a String of length 0..64 characters. origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Type ? after ipv6-address- to see the available interfaces. Runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and set interface to DCN-B. The interface you name must be bound to the same VRF as the vrf given in the static-route key. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B, alongside the DCN form add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN. Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual, special-next-hop blackhole. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (instance). direction is ingress or egress. address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the address attribute. address is the string used to identify the management address component of the remote system, length 0..64, and its purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. if-id is the interface number as an integer. address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string length 0..128.

They report the same kind of data but from different ends, and they differ in their key. management-address is keyed by lldp-port, direction, address-subtype and address: show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. management-address-local drops the direction element: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], and is used to view the management address information from the local LLDP ports (example: show management-address-local). Both run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and both expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index based on the ifIndex MIB object, or system-port-number based on the system port numbering convention), if-id as an integer, and address-oid as a string of length 0..128. For management-address-local, address-oid is currently an empty string.

Yes, the networking command has a use-as-source attribute: the interface to use as the source address. It is a string of length 0..64 and has no default. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it with show networking [use-as-source]; both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. This is the only parameter the networking command exposes.

Use show networking-services. This command shows the list of network services on the node. It takes no command parameters at all, so there is nothing to qualify or filter on the command line; you simply issue show networking-services. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and it is show-only, with no add, set or delete forms.

Because the next-hop model is anchored on the RIB. Each entry of `show next-hop` represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. So the AID is `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]`, keyed first by rib-name (String, length 1..64, pattern '([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*)'), then destination-prefix (IP prefix), then interface (outgoing interface name, for example DCN), with next-hop-address as an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`; bare `show next-hop` lists all. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>` in Operational Mode. It removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the command does not wait for completion. The instance parameter is the id of the ospf-instance, given as a string; it is mandatory. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, otherwise you are prompted. Example: `clear ospf 1`. The ospf-instance itself is created and removed from configuration with `add ospf-instance-<instance-id>` / `delete ospf-instance-<instance-id>`; the clear form is the asynchronous restart path referenced from the ospf-instance description.

No. The ospf-area object accepts only one area type: `ospf-area-type` has the single permitted value `normal`, which is also the default. Areas are managed with `add|set|show|delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>]`, where instance-id is uint8 (range 0..255) and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad OSPF Router Area ID. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0`. There is no stub, totally-stubby or NSSA option in the guide.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask, and it is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: `add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>]`, plus `show` and `delete` on the same AID. instance-id is the OSPF Router instance ID, ospf-area-id is a String, and prefix is an IPv4 prefix (length <= 32) or IPv6 prefix (length <= 128) in canonical form with non-prefix bits zero. `advertise` takes true or false and defaults to true (advertise or hide). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: `add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true`. Delete prompts for confirmation.

Yes. The `version` attribute of ospf-instance takes ospfv2 or ospfv3, defaulting to ospfv2, and it is settable only at add time (`add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]`; the set form does not carry version). The router id is controlled by `router-id-mode`, values manual or use-loopback, default use-loopback; with manual you supply `router-id` as a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback, the ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. instance-id is uint8 (range 0..255), description is a String of length 0..128, and `show` also exposes the bound vrf. Example: `add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3`.

On ospf-interface the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related timers: retransmission-interval default 5 (range 2..3600 s) and transmit-delay default 1 (range 1..450 s). Other defaults: ospf-cost 10 (range 1..65535), priority 1 (uint8 0..255, 0 means not eligible for DR/BDR), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto), ospf-network-type broadcast (show only). Authentication is available: `ospf-auth-enable` true/false, default false, relevant only for ospfv2 or ospfv3; `ospf-auth-algorithm` none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256, and `ospf-auth-key` an ASCII string of length 0..256, both relevant only for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist first.

Use `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority]` (Operational Mode). The state values are: down (initial state, no Hello packets received from neighbor), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional communication established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor (DBD) packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note: an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use the OSPFv3 IPsec security association: `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>]`, with matching set, show and delete forms. spi is a unique security parameter index, uint32 range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and takes AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 or AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol allows only ESP (default ESP) and ipsec-mode allows only transport (default transport). instance-id is uint8 0..255, ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128`.

Use `ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>`. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c=<count> stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets; -w=<timeout> is a deadline in seconds after which ping exits regardless of packets sent or received; -s=<pktsize> is the number of octets sent excluding all headers, default 56, plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. `ping -h` shows help. Access mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `show protocols`, which lists them all in one place, and then drill in per protocol: `show protocols [ssh|cli|serial-console|netconf|grpc|snmp|restconf|http-file-server|data-model-openconfig]`. Those nine are the protocols exposed. Sample values from the guide: ssh port 8022 with host keys ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521 and ssh-host-key-ssh-rsa4096 plus pre-login/post-login messages; cli enabled true, port 22, script-dir '/storage/scripts'; serial-console global-switch enabled, global-timeout 60 minutes; netconf enabled true, port 830, annotate-cli-name false; restconf enabled true, http-enabled false, https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root '/restconf'; grpc port 50051; snmp port 161 with snmp-engine-id; http-file-server http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base '/transfer'; data-model-openconfig 'OPENCONFIG model'. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so you select the address family by selecting the RIB. rib-name is a String of length 1..64, vrf is the VRF to which the RIB is bound (leafref to ../../vrf/name), and address-family shows ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Example: `show rib-IPv4` views the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]`. The `source-protocol` attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP, static. The command shows the list of system routes from various sources, such as dynamic protocols and static route. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. `special-next-hop` is the special next hop used for IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring, with values none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes), blackhole and unreachable (for both, no next-hop is created under the route); default none. Bare `show route` lists all system routes. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes: `show routing`. It shows routing information and takes no parameters at all. Access mode is Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. From there you drill down into the specific objects: `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]` for the RIBs, `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]` for the system routes and their source protocol, `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]` for next hops, and `show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]` for the routing instances.

`show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface>` shows supporting interface information, that is, which underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface supports a given interface. It has two keys: `name`, the name of the interface (string), and `interface`, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, expressed as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are show-only. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. There are no configurable attributes and no add/set/delete forms.

By default a trace probes a maximum of 30 hops and uses the MGMT VRF. Syntax: `traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]`. -m=<hopcnt> is the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live), uint8 range 1..255, default 30. -v=<vrf> is a string; if not provided it defaults to MGMT. -w=<timeout> is seconds before traceroute exits, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -i=<interface> sets the source interface (leafref to ne:networking:interface:if-name); by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probing packet size, uint16, 60 bytes for IPv4, default 60. tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name.

Use `show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]`, which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. `chassis-name` gives the associated chassis name for that VRF. `name` is the VRF name, String of length 0..32; `type` is mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF); `description` is the description of the VRF and its intended purpose, String of length 0..255. All four are show-only attributes. Example: `show vrf-MGMT` views the Management VRF attributes; bare `show vrf` lists the instances. Access mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

`activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>]` activates the currently installable software image, and a successful swimage activation implies a system restart. The optional db-action specifies what happens to the database: auto (default) processes the database with the system default behavior, empty-db activates the image with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given, you must confirm the activation when prompted; -v forces the validate check again. `label` names the sw image/manifest file; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Example: `activate swimage db-action=empty-db`. Access mode: Operational Mode.

No: only a single location led test can be running at a time, and not all cards support the Location LED test functionality. Syntax: `activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>]`, where entity is a chassis or a card. led-mode is flash (default), an amber light flashing at 1Hz, usually used for LED location, or solid, a steady amber light usually used for lamp test; in lamp test all chassis LEDs light amber. To turn it off use `terminate location-led [entity=]<value>`, or set `timeout`, a Number in the range 0..120 seconds; the default 0 means no timeout, so the function runs until terminate is issued. Note: the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there. Example: `activate location-led card-1-1`.

Use `bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>`. It establishes a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisions the initial administrator account on the neighbor, and is used during commissioning to remotely create the first administrator user on an OSC peer NE that has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either with local-port, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface (same value as in `show interface`, e.g. 1-1-dwdm-line1), or with neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (string length 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'). With local-port the system maps it to the OCE netdev OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> and resolves the peer address via get_osc_neighbors.sh; if resolution fails the RPC is rejected. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and follows local user naming rules; new-password may be a SHA512 hash ($6$salt$hash, salt 2..16 chars) or plain text subject to system complexity rules. Access mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

Type `cancel-upgrade`. The full syntax is `cancel-upgrade [-h]`, where -h displays help for the command; there are no other parameters. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully, so if nothing is running the command will not succeed. Access mode: Operational mode, and there is no candidate-configuration form and no force flag. The guide gives the example `cancel-upgrade` to cancel any active upgrade.

`change-ztp-mode enabled` starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so re-enabling it on an in-service node wipes the configuration. Syntax: `change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>`, where ztp-mode is enabled or disabled and -f forces the command without confirmation (otherwise you are prompted). `change-ztp-mode disabled` disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. The current ZTP mode can be displayed with `show ztp`. Access mode: Operational mode.

Use `show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status]` (also accepted as <card-name>.<slot-name>/<fw-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name> or <name>/<fw-name>). Compare `fw-version`, the current version, against `expected-fw-version`, the expected version, both Strings of length 0..32. `fw-status` states it directly: current means the firmware is up-to-date, not-current means it is not up-to-date against the expected one, and unavailable means firmware status information is currently unavailable; the default is unavailable. fw-name is a String of length 0..32. Bare `show current-fw` tabulates every entry, e.g. current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 vs expected 0x28 shown as not-current. Access mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

`download` supports these filetypes: crl (a CRL file in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (passphrase-protected PKCS#12, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (PKCS#12), script (a CLI script from a remote server), swimage (a manifest file, then all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; there is no need to provide a local location. The exception is filetype 'file', where `destination` may be omitted (default directory, original file-name), a file-name only, a relative path (appended to the default directory), or an absolute path within user-accessible directories; you need write access there, and `show transfer` reveals the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp. Source is a file-server plus path, or a URL using ftp, sftp, scp, http, https or file; ftp/http need secure-mode disabled.

Use `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]`, which retrieves information about downloaded image files. The `signature` attribute is the downloaded software image file signature, a String of length 0..1024. The keys are manifest-file, the downloaded manifest file and its information (String, length 0..256), and name, the name of the downloaded software image (String, length 0..256). All three are show-only. Bare `show downloaded-image` lists all downloaded software image files. Access mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

`show downloads`. It shows a list of downloads and takes no parameters. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands: `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]` for information about downloaded image files including their signature, and `show transfer-status` to check the progress of an asynchronous (-a) download or upload. Files arrive on the node via `download [-f] [-i] [-u] [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ...`, whose filetype values are crl, database, file, krp, local-certificate, peer-certificate, script, swimage and trusted-certificate; the system stores each downloaded file in an appropriate place automatically.

Yes, with the file command in Operational mode: file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>. Supported operations are rename (renames a file or directory), view (listing for a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), sha256sum (SHA256 hash of a file) and md5sum (md5 hash of a file); a result attribute reports the file operation result. new-file-path is only used for rename and is a string with pattern [A-Za-z0-9 -/.]*. Access is restricted: file system access is limited to the current user's access, so not all files and directories are editable. Examples: file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log, file view /tmp, file delete /tmp/a.log, file sha256sum /tmp/a.log. show file <filename> displays a file's contents. Separately, clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value> removes one file of type krp (only 1 krp may exist, so target-file is not needed), script (use show script to list) or swimage (a downloaded swimage not yet installed).

Both are Operational mode commands for basic file and directory operations, and both take file-path and new-file-path (a new path to the file, used for rename). The difference is the operation set. file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value> supports only rename, delete and view. file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value> supports rename, delete and view plus the two checksum operations sha256sum (SHA256 hash of a file) and md5sum (md5 hash of a file), and it also exposes a result parameter carrying the file operation result. The file entry additionally documents show file <filename> to display a file's contents and clear [-f] file <filetype> <target-file> to remove a krp, script or not-yet-installed swimage. So file is the fuller command; file-operation is the reduced rename/delete/view form.

Configure servers with add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>], edit with set file-server-<name>, view with show file-server-<name> or show file-servers, remove with delete file-server-<name>. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https. file represents local storage including USB storage and requires initial-path to be provided; ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false. Mandatory on add are server-address and protocol. server-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain name. server-port is optional; if not provided the default for the selected protocol is used. Lengths: name 0...64 characters, user-name 0..64, password 0...128, initial-path 0...256, label 0...256. Example: add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'.

Use show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is the file type for which the transfer happened. last-operation reports the direction and takes unknown, upload or download; last-completion-status is the last transfer status; last-transfer is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see set-time); last-duration is the last transfer duration as a time-interval. For a per-operation view with byte counts and progress use show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>, whose last-completion-status shows values such as success, fail, in-progress or unknown. Transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the specified filetype.

Yes, HTTP is available but it is off by default. Use set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>] and show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base], in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the master switch for file server access, true or false, default true. http-enabled enables the HTTP protocol, true or false, default false. https-enabled enables HTTPS, true or false, default true. http-port is the user configurable HTTP port, a number, default 8980. https-port is the secure HTTP port, default 8981. url-base is show-only, the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application, a string of 1..100 characters, default /transfer.

Use the manifest commands, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information] gives the file itself: manifest-signature is a hex-string of length 0..1024, downloaded-on is the download timestamp in format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and information is a string of 0..256. show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description] gives each package: state takes installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (install failed) or unknown, defaulting to unknown; version is 0..64 characters and description 0..512. show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version] lists the firmware carried per equipment-type. manifest-file is 0..256 characters, equipment-type and fw-name 0..32, name 1..256. Use show manifest for the list of manifests.

No. The packaged-fw commands show the firmware version included in a software load, and versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type. Use show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version], or show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version] without a location; show packaged-fw lists all components' firmware versions. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, a string of 0..64 characters. swload-state takes active (active software load), inactive or installable. equipment-type is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use this firmware, 0..32 characters; fw-name is the firmware name, 0..32; fw-version is the included version, 0..32. Output entries look like packaged-fw-active/CHM6/DCO-OEC and packaged-fw-active/XMM4/IOP.

Yes. prepare-upgrade prepares the NE software for upgrade and has two options: validate, which validates the software label or manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>, Operational Mode only. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. manifest is a leafref to a downloaded manifest-file. db-action is valid for unattended upgrade only and takes empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db. clear-type takes full (default), keep-networking or initialize-from-script and is only valid for an unattended operation with db-action set to empty-db. new-admin-user (0..64 chars) and new-admin-password are mandatory with keep-networking or initialize-from-script. Example: prepare-upgrade validate <label>, then prepare-upgrade apply <label>.

The command is clear [-f] recover-mode, Operational Mode, and it has no parameters; -f forces the command without confirmation. Clearing the flag clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. Because of that reconfiguration it may be traffic impacting, so treat it as a service-affecting action rather than a purely administrative one. Examples: clear recover-mode, or clear -f recover-mode to skip the confirmation prompt.

Use show software-load-<swload-state> or show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state takes active (active software load), inactive, or installable. Selectable attributes are swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-information, swload-activation-type, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false) are only of relevance for the installable load, as is swload-activation-type, which takes direct (no reboot type determined), warmstart (update requires warm reboot) or coldstart. swload-status covers status-unknown, validate-in-progress/complete/failed/timeout, apply-in-progress/complete/failed/timeout, activate-in-progress/complete/failed/timeout and cancel-in-progress/complete/failed/timeout. Examples: show software-load-active, show software-load-1-5/active.

Use show software-location-<location-id>, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, where location-id is the location of the equipment as a string of 0..64 characters, given as chassis-slot. For example show software-location-1-5 retrieves software location information from the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To narrow to a particular load on that slot, go through sw-management: show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable], for example show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active, which returns software-load-1-4/active with its sw-component entries, swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. The equivalent direct form is show software-load-1-5/active.

Use show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply and are strings of length 1...20. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by this subtype, in gbps. max-capacity is the maximum capacity supported, in gbps, where -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications is the list of applications supported by this subtype and unsupported-applications the list not supported, both of application type; if either list is empty then that constraint is not applicable. description is the subtype description, a string of length 1...255.

Use show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description], or show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> without a location, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The state parameter is the package state and takes installed (software package installed), not-installed (software package not installed), installation-failed (software package install failed) or unknown (software package state unknown); the default is unknown. So a component that failed to install shows state installation-failed. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, 0..64 characters; swload-state is active, inactive or installable; name is the package name, 0..256 characters; version is 0..64 and description 0..512. Examples: show sw-component to list all, or show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg for one package.

Use show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime], in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; show sw-container lists all OS-level containers with their attributes. cpu-usage is the container's current CPU usage as a number in the range 0 ...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates overall usage relative to all cores. memory-usage is the current memory usage as a percentage in the range 0 ...100%. state takes off (default state, container not launched yet), up (container is up and running) or exited. equipment is a leafref to the equipment/card AID on which the container is running, description is a brief description of the container instance, and uptime is the time since the container started. Example: show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi. Per-service figures come from show sw-service, which also has cpu-usage and memory-usage.

Yes, with service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure. Use add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>, set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>], show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action] and delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string of 0..64 characters. fail-action takes default-action, which performs the policy of restarting the service and then rebooting the system if the service is not recovered; ignore, meaning no automatic action is taken on service failure; or system-restart, which performs a warm restart of the system or card software immediately upon service failure. Example: add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action.

Yes, show sw-management, which shows information about software locations, activity and downloads, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]. downloads shows the download history, listing the manifest files downloaded. software-location-<shelf>-<slot> shows software loads by shelf and slot and accepts software-load-active, software-load-inactive or software-load-installable. software-load-active shows active software and software-load-inactive shows inactive software; the active view lists the sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. Examples: show sw-management downloads, show sw-management software-load-active, show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active.

Use show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count], or show sw-services for all services and containers on the node; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. reboot-count is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16, so a high or climbing value indicates a service restarting repeatedly. Cross-check last-start-time, the time of the last service start or boot, as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and uptime, the time since the service turned up, in days:hours:minutes. state takes off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with state-details giving a brief description. sv-name is a unique id per service instance containing card type, shelf and slot, for example show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr.

sw-subcomponent drills one level below sw-component: it shows the software load subcomponent details, keyed by the component name plus the subcomponent name. Syntax: show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description], or show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> without a location; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. sw-component only keys on <location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>. The attributes are the same in both: state takes installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown, default unknown; version is 0..64 characters; description is 0..512. sw-component-name is 1..256 and sw-subcomponent-name 1..256; location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, 0..64. Example: show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb, versus show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg.

Run swversion. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element. The syntax is just swversion, it takes no parameters, and it is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists both the NE-level loads and the per-location loads with their version and label, for example software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188, software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112, software-load-installable, then software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable. For the full attribute set on any one of those loads use show software-load-<swload-state>, and for locations, downloads and load state together use show sw-management.

Use show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt], in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. file-status is the firmware file status and takes valid, invalid or missing. crc is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, a string of 0...64. applicable-eqpt is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to, with max-elements 80, while present-in-eqpt is the list of resources that contain this version, also max-elements 80. path is the path for the firmware image, 0...255; version 0...64; vendor 0...64; part-number 0...64; nsa-upgrade-version lists the versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting, 0...255.

Set it on the transfer object: set transfer [http-proxy <value>], and read it back with show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]; Operational and Candidate configuration mode. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Important restriction: this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of 0..1024 characters in the format [http://]<host>[:<port>], where http:// is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional; if <port> is omitted the default is 1080. Example: set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080.

Use show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details], in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. operation is upload or download. transfer-progress is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100 percent, default 0; bytes-transferred is a uint64 byte count, default 0; total-bytes is the total file size in bytes and is zero until known at the transfer start, default 0. details gives the transfer phase: idle (default), preparation, transfer, completed or Failed. last-completion-status is a 0..128 string such as success, fail, in-progress or unknown; unknown can occur if the system reboots while a transfer is in progress. transfer-type is sync or async. Transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the filetype. In synchronous mode a live progress bar is rendered in the CLI; with -a use this command.

Use show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details], in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. It displays all SW versions being installed and their installation status, reported at NE level, chassis level and card level; resource is a string of 0..255 identifying the entire ne, a chassis or a card, and for ne and chassis the results are aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope. A partial failure shows status upgrade-partially-failed at the aggregate level, so drill into the chassis and card resources to find which one shows apply-failed, validate-failed, activate-failed, cancel-failed or no-communication. Other status values are idle (default), upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/complete, apply-in-progress/complete, activate-in-progress/complete and cancel-in-progress/complete. step identifies the current upgrade step (0..128) with step-start-time; start-time and end-time show na if the entity was idle or finished no phase since startup; details is 0..255. to-swload-version is the target load.

Use upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ... in Operational mode. For diagnostics use filetype=debug-log, which uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs; debug-entity is a mandatory parameter and restricts the logs to a particular card or chassis, and optional-content (string 0..64) adds optional content. Related types are logs, pm-logs (with period 15min/24h), fdr-log and otdr-result. Destination is either a configured file-server plus path, or a URL <protocol>://[<user>@]<address>[:<port>]/<path>/<filename> with ftp, sftp, scp, http, https or file; ftp and http only work when secure-mode is disabled. -a runs it asynchronously (check with show transfer-status), -s skips TLS or ssh known-host verification. Certificates differ: for local-certificate and peer-certificate you must specify certificate-name; for trusted-certificate omitting the name exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and output files are in P7 pem format.

Use show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status], in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; configuration is done with change-ztp-mode. ztp-mode is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled, default enabled, and is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC which is allowed even when the NBI is locked. ztp-state is the current state of the ZTP service and progresses through ztp-init (the default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress and ztp-completed, with ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart as the other values. ztp-details gives additional information on the current state, a string of 0..256. ztp-completion-status is the summarized completion status on the node, not-completed (default) or completed.

Use the capabilities command: 'show capabilities-<name>', where <name> is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the capability information for that particular card. It is a show-only command, available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show capabilities-1-4. If you want capability data by card type rather than for one installed card, use the type-level capability commands instead: supported-card (per card-type), supported-slot (per slot), supported-port (per port) and supported-tom / supported-tom-power (per pluggable).

Provisioning uses 'add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>', with optional [required-subtype] [card-mode] [subslot-name] [power-profile] [alias-name] [admin-state] [alarm-report-control] [label]. required-type is the card type, String length 0..32, for example CHM1R, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, XMM4, UTM2, RD20TM, FAN, FAN-CTRL, PEM, IOPANEL, SPN2, BLANK. chassis-name is String 1...255 (default 1) and slot-name is a String. required-subtype applies to FAN (counter-rotating, single-rotor), PEM (AC, DC), PAxOFP2 (ER default, LR, IR), RPBM (MP4, MP5), RPBL (LS2, MP6) and CHM6 (C4, C6, C8, C9, C13, C14, C15). subslot-name can only be set on (sub)card creation. admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control to Inhibited. Example: add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2.

On 1830 GX G40 you must set the chassis ambient temperature to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If that parameter is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. The attribute is configured-ambient-temperature on the chassis object: 'set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature 40'. Its value is a number in Celsius units with no default, and it is used to compute the FRU power consumption. It is available in add, set and show on chassis-<name>, in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'set console-<name> baud-rate <value>' and 'show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state] [local-switch] [status]'. Permitted baud-rate values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: in auto-sensing mode the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, locks it, and reports it in actual-baud-rate. auto-sensing-state shows sensing or locked (default sensing) and is only visible if auto-sensing is enabled on that port. Not all cards support auto-sensing; supported-card console-port-support reports no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate or yes-with-fixed-baud-rate.

Use 'show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]'. redundancy-standby-status is the one to check: ready-synchronized means the standby controller is in sync and ready. The other values are not-ready-synchronizing (standby is synchronizing data with the active controller, and is the default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out state) and card-not-present. redundancy-status reports active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card; additional-details is a string 0..128 giving further synchronization detail. Example: show controller-card-1-12.

Use 'show equipment [<option>]' to display installed equipment information; the available options vary with your installation. With no option it lists the installed equipment; with an option it narrows to one object, for example 'show equipment card-1-1'. That output shows the card plus its child objects (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-AUX-2, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) and the card attributes: required-type (XMM4), required-subtype, category (controller), chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw (58.80 W), last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state (unlock), oper-state (enabled), avail-state ('normal in-service'), alarm-report-control and label. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Both are controlled by equipment-policies: 'set equipment-policies [tom-auto-migration <value>] [auto-assigned-directions <value>] [auto-assigned-degrees <value>] [cable-id-control <value>] [chassis-assignment-mode <value>] [comm-eth-location <value>]'. tom-auto-migration (enabled/disabled) enables automatic update of the tom subtype based on the present equipment; it can directly impact existing configurations, and it covers subtype migration only, not tom type migration (no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are not automatic by default: auto-assigned-degrees (enabled/disabled) defaults to disabled, and is enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. auto-assigned-directions defaults to enabled. Example: set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled.

You have to enable them. The global switch is use-serdes-templates on equipment-templates: 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>' and 'show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates'. Values are enabled/disabled (the CLI value completion offers false and true) and the default is disabled. On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively to what is already there; they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact: existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, whether it was applied via template or manually. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being set to 'true'; you can force re-application with the apply-template command.

Use the fru-info command: 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. It displays the packaged FRU information associated to a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Neither has a default. The command is show-only and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the inventory command, which shows inventory data for a present FRU: 'show inventory-<name> [serial-number] [clei] ...'. The AID can be inventory-<name>, inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>, inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name> or inventory-<card-name>-<port-name> for a pluggable. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment (String) and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier (String). Other attributes available on the same command: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code (string 0...18, for 3rd party TOMs), actual-power-class (uint8, 1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status. Example: show inventory-1-3-1.

Use 'show led-<location>/<name> [status]', or 'show leds' for the whole list. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID), String 1..32; name is the LED name within the FRU, String 1..16. The status attribute gives the current colour state, with values: not-available (default), off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycling through all supported colours including off), cycling (cycling excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. Yes, the object exists even if the FRU is not physically present; such LEDs simply report not-available. Example entries: led-1-1/active green, led-1-1/fault off.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three types of ports: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports are seen on a CHM6 or a CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is present/provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The port-type attribute (show only) reports: line (line-side 'coloured' CWDM/DWDM module), tributary (grey client interface), tributary-subport (tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports connecting to an adjunct line function), optical, otdr, pluggable (port entity representing the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM) and ocm. Use 'show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type', or 'show port' for all.

Use 'show resources-<name> [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth] [supported-carriers] [unassigned-carriers] [supported-sub-components]'. The bandwidth attributes are applicable only to SPN2/SPN2C cards. internal-cell-switch-total/available-bandwidth default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. paired-slot-total/available-bandwidth apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots, and default to 500.000 Gbit/s with that capability, or 0 without it. Example: show resources-254-1 giving internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth 358.750 Gbit/s and paired-slot-available-bandwidth 258.750 Gbit/s.

Read the status attribute on the serdes object: 'show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]'. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values: set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown, the default), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). 'show serdes' lists every serdes with its value and status, for example serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ value 1 status set. Configure with 'add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>' or 'set ... value <value>'; 'delete' removes the serdes from the configuration.

A serdes-template is created per tom-part-number (string, length 1..16) and applies to all line cards that support serdes; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Scope by port is set with ports-applicable: 'all' if all ports are to be considered (the default) or a list of port names, string length 1..16, maximum 20 elements (for example T1..T16). Syntax: 'add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]' and 'set serdes-template-<tom-part-number> [ports-applicable <value>]'. Manual serdes configuration is still possible and is kept even if it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Application depends on use-serdes-templates being 'true'; apply-template forces re-application.

Each individual parameter is a serdes-template-entry, composed of a serdes parameter name and its associated value: 'add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>'. Edit with 'set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]', remove with 'delete ...', and view with 'show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]'. name is the name of the serdes parameter, string length 0....256; value is the value of the serdes parameter, string length 0...256; tom-part-number is string length 1..16. Examples: add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3; set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The serial-console object holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system: 'set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]' and 'show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]'. global-switch allows access by serial console, values enabled/disabled, default enabled; each console port can override this global behaviour (see the per-card console local-switch, with use-global-switch, force-enable, force-disable). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes, default 60, and can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80.

Use 'show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]' (or 'show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>' for a subslot); 'show slot' lists them all. current-equipment is the name of the equipment currently required in this slot, for example 1-1, and shows --- when none. supported-type lists the types the holder accepts (for example CHM6,gx:UCM4), and installed-type is the type actually present, empty when no FRU is fitted. oper-state is enabled or disabled, avail-state gives values such as 'normal in-service' or 'partially-faulted abnormal in-service'. For the type-level view of what could go there, use supported-slot possible-card-types.

Use 'show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]'; 'show sub-component' with no key lists all of them. card-name is the name of the card supporting the sub-component, string length 0..64; sub-component-name is the name of the sub-component (string); AID is the Resource Access Identifier, string length 1..64; description is a user configurable description of the sub-component, string length 0..128. Example output: sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec and description 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component', and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc, AID 1-6-dco-secproc, 'DCO Security Processor sub-component'. The names present on a card are also listed by resources supported-sub-components, which can be addressed for operations such as restart.

Use 'show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility'. Node Type Compatibility refers to the supported NE node-type for a sled card, and is only of relevance for line-card(s) and carrier-card(s). The values are: all (compatibility with any node-type), ILA (compatibility with the In-Line Amplifier, two-directions node type) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer node type). So a card usable on an in-line amplifier node reports all or ILA. The same command also gives supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Example: show supported-card-CHM1R.

Use 'show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> [controller-redundancy-supported] [number-of-front-slots] [number-of-rear-slots] ...'; chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis supports controller redundancy. Slot counts come from number-of-front-slots (equipment holder slots in the front plate) and number-of-rear-slots (slots in the back plate), both uint8. The same command reports supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, power-control-supported, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (not-applicable, optional-dust-filter default, dust-filter-regularly-replaced), depth in mm, height in RUs, leds, supported-subchassis-type (max 10 elements) and supported-features. Example: G42 reports controller-redundancy-supported true, 7 front slots, 12 rear slots, depth 600 mm, height 3 RUs.

Use 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> [port-type] [direction] [configuration-mode] [faceplate-label] [leds] [present] [default-tom] [parent-port] [subport-list] [allows-auto-migration]', for example show supported-port-CHM1R/2. port-type says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, pluggable or ocm. configuration-mode says who provisions it: system-configured (the system automatically configures the card in slot / TOM in port and the user cannot make changes) or user-configured (the user can provision or de-provision). Also useful: present (always, or in-node-controller-only), default-tom (default none), faceplate-label (string 1..36), leds (max 10 elements), and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true), which says whether TOMs plugged on this port type are auto migrated per the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag.

Use 'show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>' (or supported-slot-<card-type>/<slot-name>) with [requires-blank-when-empty] [possible-card-types] [configuration-mode] [auto-provision-capable] [default-card] [slot-location] [slot-vertical-position] [slot-horizontal-position] [reset-power] [virtual-slot] [leds]. requires-blank-when-empty tells you whether a BLANK filler card is needed when the slot is empty, with values not-applicable, optional and required. possible-card-types is the list of card types allowed in that slot, an identityref list with a maximum of 15 elements. configuration-mode is system-configured or user-configured, auto-provision-capable is true/false, default-card names the card present by default, reset-power is the reset power consumption at 55degC in W, and virtual-slot defaults to false. On a G42 for example, slots 1, 3, 4-7 and PEM-1..4 show required, while IOPANEL, FAN and FANCTRL slots show not-applicable.

Use 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]'. It gives the capability information for a supported TOM in the scope of a particular card. card-type is for example CHM1R, tom-type is the form factor such as CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD, and tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32 such as '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode lists the phy-modes supported for that TOM on that card, and default-phy-mode gives the one used by default; the possible values are 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G. Examples: show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28, show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout.

Use 'show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]'. tom-type is the pluggable form factor (TOM type identity matching the TOM required-type, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD). supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, a uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so also read supported-max-power-draw, the maximum power in watts the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class (decimal64). To compare against what the fitted module reports, read actual-power-class (uint8 1..8) and actual-max-power-draw on the inventory object; those are only populated for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules, not for native qualified subtypes.

Yes. When you create a TOM with `add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>`, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. The add takes required-type (CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP, SFPPLUS) plus optional required-subtype (0..32 chars), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (true/false, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; CHM7 cards only). Example: `add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD`. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the tom-type command: `show tom-type-<tom-type> [data-rate] [description] [support-third-party-toms] [generic-subtype]`. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (true/false) that says whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to supported Nokia TOMs; generic-subtype gives the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. Other read-only attributes are description (0..255 chars), tom-type (identityref) and data-rate (uint16, Gbps). `show tom-type` alone lists all supported types. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) is used to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It shows up under unprovisioned-inventory, which lists detected inventory not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. Use `show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name> [hardware-version] [actual-type] [actual-subtype] [sw-support-revision] [PON] [serial-number] [clei] [vendor] [part-number] [manufacture-date] [detection-timestamp]`. The AID is chassis-serial-number (string 0..16) plus slot-name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. detection-timestamp is the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment, in date-and-time form; manufacture-date uses YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]`. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as a target or source for file transfer operations (String, 0..32). available-space is the current free space and total-space the total space, both uint16 in MB. These three are applicable only when type is storage; type is either storage (file storage and associated file management operations) or power-supply (powers external equipment such as passive shelves). present indicates the connector presence (true/false, default false). `show usb` lists all USB ports on the node, e.g. `show usb-1-5-U1` for the FRCU card. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` from Operational mode. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp; db-paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated, a string of length 40...200; sanity-check-override defaults to false and is set to true to override the sanity check. Pre-condition: a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated, so run take-snapshot first. Examples: `activate-snapshot onehour` activates the snapshot named onehour, and `activate-snapshot sanity-check-override` activates while overriding the sanity check. Existing snapshots can be listed with `show database`.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after `enable-advanced-parameters` is set to true on the optical carrier; that attribute takes true/false and defaults to false, so with it left at false your setting does not take effect. Also, if no advanced parameter is configured, or the parameter was deleted, `show advanced-parameter` reports `ERROR: object does not exist`. Note that an advanced parameter configured with an invalid value is not rejected: `show advanced-parameter` then reports status `failed` for it. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown (default unknown). Syntax is `add|set|show|delete advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>`.

Use `apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])`. With template-type serdes-template (the default value shown for the parameter is serdes-templage) the command applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOMs given in the applicable-tom list. applicable-tom is a comma-separated list of TOMs to apply the serdes-templates against; if it is not provided, that is, the list is empty, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Other parameters may be required depending on the template type. Example: `apply-template serdes-template` applies to every TOM, `apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1` restricts it to that TOM. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]` from Candidate Configuration mode (entered with `configure`).
