The candidate is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a 'persist' trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm with `commit persist` or abort with `commit cancel`. A Persistent Confirmed Commit requires the -id parameter, which defines the ID shared by the commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel commands. `commit -m=<message>` attaches a custom message.

Use `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]`. It displays the system's configuration, skipping any configuration left at its default value, and the output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. You can narrow it by passing an <entity-id>, or an <entity-type> if all entities of that type are relevant. To get it back as replayable CLI, the guide's recommendation is `show config | display commands`, storing the result for later use as a script that restores the system configuration; see the display command for details. Such a stored script can then be fed back with `configure from-script=<script>`.

It depends on the target you pick. `configure <target>` moves from operational mode into Candidate Configuration mode, where target is exclusive or shared and defaults to exclusive. In exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can change the candidate configuration. Example: `configure exclusive`. The same command sets the candidate's starting point: by default the candidate starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; `from-default` starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration; `from-script=<script>` imports a configuration from a text file of CLI commands; `from-commit=<commit-id>` starts from a past commit-record, available only when the Commit Repository is available, meaning the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled.

Use `show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]`, which shows the current values of the advanced parameters that are running on the system, as opposed to the configured values reported by `show advanced-parameter`. The keys are optical-carrier-name and current-advanced-parameter-name, both strings, and value is the string value running on the system. `show current-advanced-parameter` lists them all; `show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*` restricts output to one optical carrier. The running value can differ from the configured value, for example PMDEquUpdSpeed shows 20 as the running value rather than the configured one; PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified and is to be supported in a future release. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. `clear database` performs a full wipe of the database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; use the `clear system` command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Three clear-type actions exist: full (reset to factory defaults, the default), keep-networking (full wipe but network configurations kept), and initialize-from-script (full wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Use -f to skip confirmation. Ignore transient alarms raised after the controller card reboot.

Use `db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>`, which defines the protection mode to be configured. type takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption; encryption-with-integrity is the one that adds integrity protection on top of encryption. -f forces the command without confirmation. Access is Operational Mode. Example: `db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity` enables the integrity check for the system database and automatically reboots the controller. Verify the result with `show db-protection-scheme`, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is documented as changeable via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm then shows hmac-sha2-512 instead of none.

Use `show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]` and read integrity-status, which reports passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup, or disabled. The other attributes are encryption-algorithm, which is xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size; integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. All four are show-only. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. On a node still in encryption-only, integrity-algorithm reads none and integrity-status reads disabled.

Use `diff [-t|-c] candidate`, run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore configuration and the current system configuration, covering created, deleted and changed objects and showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate, 'old' data is the current system configuration. Default output is normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values. -t gives a side-by-side (table) diff, and -c gives the changes as CLI commands you could execute to make the same configuration; -d gives the list of commands being executed. You can also compare commit-records with `diff commit <id> [<id>]`, available when commit-tracking is enabled or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run `discard-changes` from Candidate Configuration mode. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags. Access Mode is Candidate Configuration mode only, so it is not available from operational mode. If instead you want to keep working but start the candidate over, re-enter with `configure <exclusive|shared> from-default` for a blank config, or use `rollback commit` against an empty candidate to initialize it from a past commit-record.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care: it requires you to know the extended-config name, and the name must match a name already known by the system. The commands are `add extended-config-<name>`, `delete extended-config-<name>` and `show extended-config-<name> [description]`. name is a String of length 0..64 and is the entity key; description is a String of length 0..255 that displays the description of the extended-config provided by the system and its effect in the system, so use the show to read what a given name actually does before adding it. Access Mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Check the Golden Advanced Parameter Table (GAPT) entry with `show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]`. service-impact is the attribute that answers this: it is service-affecting or non-service-affecting, and if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock/maintenance operation or other relevant operations before applying. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change, or full-config-no-pll-change. direction is transmit, receive or transmit-and-receive; multiplicity (uint8) is how many values you must enter. All attributes are read-only. Example: `show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/*`.

Run `lock` from Operational Mode. It locks database access to your current session, granting exclusive write access to that CLI session, and is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session already holds one. The lock is released either by the `unlock` command or by closing the session that took the lock, explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or by inactivity time-out. Only the session that performed the lock can unlock; unlocking a non-locked database or one locked by another session fails. After unlock, any session may configure or take a new lock. Both commands accept -h for help.

A named-value-set is addressed by two keys, the database entry name and the set name: `named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`. db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set; both are used in add, set, show and delete. What it holds is the value attribute, a value item that is a String of length 1..1024 characters. Full syntax: `add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]`, `set ... [value <value>]`, `show ... [value]`, and `delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`. Access Mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Only if recovery from chassis storage is configured for it. Use `set recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage <value>]` and `show recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage] [restore-status] [backup-status] [last-backup] [next-backup]`. restore-from-chassis-storage takes disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, after which you run a manual `clear recover-mode` so you can validate the restored system before affecting the HW), or auto-in-service (same restore, but the NC automatically leaves recovery mode on success). The default is auto-in-service. restore-status tracks progress: init (default), image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore. backup-status is successful, failed, in-progress or unknown.

Not while the candidate holds changes. `rollback commit [<commit-id>]` works in the Running Datastore by default or in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if the candidate is empty, which is a way to initialize the candidate. So discard your staged changes first, or roll back from operational mode against the running datastore. If no commit-id is given, the most recent commit-record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record and replays them in order, from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access Mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show commit` retrieves commit record information and lets you visualize the Commit Repository, but it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither is true on your node there are no records to show. Enable it with `set system-policies commit-tracking enabled`; note that disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records, and its default is disabled. Syntax is `show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]`, where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -n selects an exact number of records to obtain, and -s takes a timestamp and shows all records created since it. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]` and `show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]`. commit-tracking enables the commit-repository feature: with it enabled, all configuration changes done via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back. Values are enabled/disabled, default disabled, and disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled; disabling writable-running makes configuration via the running datastore impossible and forces the candidate datastore: the CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 become read-only.

The db-passphrase. The system only accepts take-snapshot if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of the security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or locally as a parameter of the command, for example `take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`. The passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and allows special characters from the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax: `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, run from Operational Mode. db-instance is temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is 0...128 characters. Re-taking an existing instance such as oneweek overwrites the existing file.

Use the template command. A template is a single template entry: an object/attribute pair plus the value to be used as the default for that attribute. Syntax: add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]. object is the object name to apply to (e.g. odu), attribute the attribute name (e.g. admin-state), and value the value to apply (e.g. lock) and is mandatory. label and condition are optional; condition restricts the rule (e.g. service-type=OTU4). sequence-id is a number in range 1..65535 and defines processing order, lower ids first. set, show and delete use the same AID. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN.

No. A template-group is a configuration group containing a list of template entries, added with add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. The enabled attribute takes true or false, and its default of true applies only if there is no other template-group enabled, so only one group holds the enabled state. Use show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label] to see which group is enabled, and delete template-group-<name> to remove one. label is an optional user label. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-group-1 adds and enables a template-group.

Use show templates. It shows the configuration that defines the data model for system templates, giving the overall view of templates on the node. The command takes no parameters. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. For the levels below it, use show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label] for an individual template-group and show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition] for an individual template entry.

No. The unlock command releases a database previously locked with the lock command, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a non-locked database, or a database locked by another session, the unlock command will fail. A lock is automatically released if the session that performed the lock is closed, so ending that operator's session frees the database. Syntax: unlock [-h], where -h displays help for this command. Access: Operational Mode. After the unlock, any session can perform configurations and take a new lock.

Yes. Use validate candidate <candidate> command <string>. It validates the contents of the specified configuration, covering any CLI command used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging or replacing content. candidate is the candidate datastore that is the target for validation; command is the command to validate, given as a string. If the command is validated, the command replies with OK; otherwise the command will fail. Multiple CLI commands can be provided if separated with a semicolon. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: validate 'set ne altitude 600'.

A maximum of 7 rounds of additional-key-exchange can be configured, with additional-key-exchange-id in range 1..7, and a unique key-exchange algorithm must be chosen for each round. The rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Syntax: add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. Configuration is optional; Child SA (port level) key exchange is derived from IKE, and configuring it takes the IKE session down immediately to renegotiate. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm; ml-kem-1024 is recommended.

Use show data-path-encryption. This command shows the datapath encryption attributes. It takes no parameters. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. The related global policy is set with set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>, values match or ignore, which controls whether the NE validates the certificate subject alternate name against the IKE ID.

Use the encryption-algorithm command, where the algorithm and key-length are part of the AID: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>, or without the SPD entry: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>. algorithm values: null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16, chacha20-poly1305. key-length values: none, key-length-128, key-length-192, key-length-256, default none. number is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Only add, show and delete are available. Example: add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192.

With ike-sa-proposal, integrity-algorithm and dh-group are mandatory on add and prf is optional: add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number> integrity-algorithm <value> dh-group <value> [prf <value>]. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf values: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. number is the proposal number, range 1..max. protocol-id is read-only, value IKE. Example: add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192.

The top-level ikev2 object carries one attribute, data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate the certificate subject alternate name to match the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore. Syntax: set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>] and show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match.

Use show ikev2-local-instance-<name> host-card-encryption-capability. It indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance is running supports the ability to do encryption; values are yes, no, unknown, default unknown. host-card is a read-only reference to the service card running the instance. The address is chosen by local-address-assignment-method, a read-only attribute with values auto and manual, default auto; local-address is the local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, and is settable. Other settable attributes: scope (data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method), label, admin-state (lock, maintenance, unlock, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited, default Inhibited). Example: set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132.

On ikev2-peer, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800; re-auth-frequency is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200. The stated rule is that re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency must not be multiples of each other, and they must have a difference of a few minutes to ensure a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Related attributes: re-key-fail-policy (kill traffic, continue traffic, default continue-traffic) with re-key-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds default 0, and re-auth-fail-policy with re-auth-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds default 0, which give the delay before killing the SAs tied to this IKE SA. Set with set ikev2-peer-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name> [re-key-frequency <value>] [re-auth-frequency <value>].

Use ipsec-sa-proposal. dh-group is mandatory and integrity-algorithm is optional on add: add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. protocol-id is show-only with value ESP (default ESP), and esn is show-only with value esn. number is the proposal number, range 1..max; ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32. Example: add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256.

Yes. Use ipsec-sa-re-key, which re-keys the IPsec child SA on time, bytes or packets: add ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> [frequency <value>] [bytes <value>] [packets <value>]. frequency is the time-based rekeying frequency, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. bytes is the rekeying frequency based on amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. packets is based on amount of packets transmitted, values disabled or a number in range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. set, show and delete take the same AID. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

On ipsec-spd-entry, the action attribute indicates the IPsec treatment given to the IP datagrams. Values are protect, bypass and discard, with default protect. The mode attribute indicates whether the IPsec session operates in transport or tunnel mode; values tunnel and transport, default tunnel, so it does tunnel by default. Syntax: add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <value> [description <value>] [action <value>] [ipsec-protocol <value>] [mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [esn <value>] [anti-replay-window <value>] [dynamic-ts <value>]. priority is mandatory (uint8) and gives precedence between SPD entries. ipsec-protocol is ESP; esn true/false default true; anti-replay-window applies when action = protect, range 32..1024, default 64; dynamic-ts disabled/enabled, default disabled; alarm-report-control allowed/inhibited, default allowed. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

Create an ipsec-traffic-selector under the SPD entry, then attach addresses and ports to it. add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]. next-layer-protocol indicates the inner (upper layer) protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field; values any (value 0), opaque (value 255), or a number in range 0-255, default any. The addresses and ports are then added as separate objects keyed under this selector: local-subnet and remote-subnet for the prefixes, and local-ports and remote-ports for the port ranges. ipsec-traffic-selector-name is a string of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Example: add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17.

Because the start and stop ports are part of the AID, not attributes. The local-ports object is addressed as local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and only add, show and delete are provided; there is no set form. To change a range, delete the entry and add the new one. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port-number with default 0, and 0 is only accepted by the system if the starting port is set to all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all, and for an individual port with start=stop=53, add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53.

Use the local-subnet command, with the prefix as part of the AID: add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, broadcast for IPv4 only). Only add, show and delete are available, so to change a subnet you delete and re-add it. ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32 and ipsec-traffic-selector-name a string of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32.

That is governed by link-security-control on macsec-entity, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. Values are must-secure and should-secure, with default must-secure, so by default traffic is not passed unprotected. Syntax: set macsec-entity-<name> [enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [link-security-control <value>] [replay-protection <value>] [replay-protection-window <value>]. enabled is true/false, default true; replay-protection is enable/disable; replay-protection-window is the number of packets to consider, range 0..4294967295, default 0; alarm-report-control is allowed/inhibited, default Inhibited. supporting-facility names the supporting facility. Example: add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3.

Use macsec-mka: set macsec-mka-<name> [connectivity-association-key <value>] [connectivity-association-key-name <value>] [mka-policy <value>] [psk-lifetime <value>] [psk-expiration-warning <value>] [psk-lifetime-enable <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. connectivity-association-key is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and connectivity-association-key-name its name, both strings of length 0..64. To see which end is key server, use show macsec-mka-<name> is-key-server: it identifies if the local end is key server, values true and false, default false. psk-expiration-warning is in range 1..173 with default 14 days, psk-lifetime-enable is enabled/disabled, and psk-configured-timestamp shows when the PSK was configured. Example: set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa.

On the mka-policy object, which is the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity related to an ethernet facility: add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. macsec-cipher-suite gives the cipher suites for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation, listed with values true, false and default true. sak-rekey-interval is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range '0|30..65535', default 30s. key-server-priority is the key server priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key-server. confidentiality-offset specifies a number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent in unencrypted plain-text, listed with values allowed, inhibited and default Inhibited. Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the re-auth command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>, where ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), given as a string. Access Mode: Operational mode. Examples: re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202, and re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2. The scheduled interval is separate: re-auth-frequency on ikev2-peer, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200.

The re-key command performs an on-demand re-key on any of three targets: a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec child security association (Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>. ipsec-security-association points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and secure-entity points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all are strings. Access Mode: Operational mode. Examples: re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1 and re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX.

Set the starting port to all on the remote-ports object: add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>. start takes all, opaque or a port number. stop is a port-number with default 0; if the stopping port is not set the system assumes 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque, so all can be given on its own. Only add, show and delete are available. Examples: add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all for every port, and add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49 for a single port.

Use the remote-subnet command, with the prefix carried in the AID: add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, broadcast for IPv4 only). Only add, show and delete exist, so a change means delete then add. It hangs off an existing ipsec-traffic-selector under an ipsec-spd-entry; ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32 and ipsec-traffic-selector-name a string of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Access: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32.

Use the sc-rx command, which shows Receiving Secure Channel attributes. Syntax: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack and takes two values: in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and not-in-use, meaning no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use. name is the entity name, a string of length 0..64; index is the Receiving Secure Channel Index, a uint8; sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier as a hex-string of length 16. sc-rx is show-only: there is no add, set or delete form. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is read-only: the only form is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. There is no add, set or delete for sc-tx, so it cannot be configured; the values are reported by the MKA stack. name is the entity name, a string of length 0..64; index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index, a uint8; sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16; state is either in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, or not-in-use, meaning none are in use. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign the certificate with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>, where id is a string of length 0..20 and active-certificate-id is a string of length 0..128 that may list several certificates, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. The in-use attribute is a leafref to ../active-certificate-id and shows the certificate actually active. To require a client certificate, set verify-client-cert, which enables or disables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled means no client certificate is requested, required means the client certificate is required and validated. Default is disabled; for TLS Mutual Authentication it must be required. Changes only affect new TLS connections, not existing ones. show secure-application-<id> reports type (server or client), status (enabled or disabled), active-certificate-id, in-use and verify-client-cert; show secure-applications lists them all.

Only if you tell it to. The secure-entity attribute re-key-fail-policy indicates the NE policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Its values are kill-traffic and continue-traffic, and the default is continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to this IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0, that is, immediately. Related, re-key-frequency is 3600..86400 seconds with a default of 28800. All three can be given on add secure-entity-<name> or changed later with set secure-entity-<name>, for example add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity 1-4-L1-1 re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. There is no add or set form, and every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521, the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. The proposal number is likewise the single value 1, defaulting to 1, and name is the proposal name for the secure entity SA. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the IKE peer itself. Commands: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], plus matching set, show and delete forms. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance; ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object, that is the IKE SA; associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). All three are strings with no stated default. Example: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with a manually configured CRL Distribution Point (CDP); each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], with set, show, delete cdp, delete cdp-<name> and show cdps. url is an HTTP URL in the form http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, host being an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the file conventionally having a .crl extension, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh and immediately triggers a CRL auto-download; when disabled no refresh occurs but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval is either the enum use-next-update, taking the time from the current CRL next-update field, or a duration written as [xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs], for example 2w or 5d 12h or 1h 7m 30s. show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Privilege level is System Administrator.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate in Operational mode: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. Validity is set by days, the number of days a certificate is valid for, and the default is 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string of length 1..64, common-name the IP or host name identifying the server, string 1..64, and subject the full certificate subject name, string 1..1024. You must specify either subject or common-name when generating the self-signed certificate. auto-install (true, false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, a prioritized set of rules that map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Use add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], with set, show and delete forms. map-type is either extract, to take the identity from a designated certificate field, or map, to use an explicit username. field applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked; priority ranges 1 to 255; issuer adds a restriction filtering certificates from a specific issuer, value any; enabled is True or False, default True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Delete with clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, run from Operational mode; -f forces without confirmation, otherwise the CLI prompts Are you sure? [y/n]. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128, which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to list the certificate-ids that can be cleared. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY. type also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, use show certificates, which displays all managed local, trusted and peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value> and pick the right clear-target. The choices are single-crl, the default, which removes only the CRL named in <crl-name> (for single-crl the crl-name is mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL); purge-invalid-crls, which purges all invalid CRLs; purge-cached-crls, which purges all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension; and purge-all-crls, which purges every CRL. So to drop stale ones only, use clear crl purge-invalid-crls; purge-all-crls would take the good ones too. Press <tab> for the list of clearable CRL names; otherwise crl-name should be omitted. Check status first with show crls or show crl-<name>, whose status attribute is valid, expired or future, and whose type attribute is cached or manually. Access Mode is Operational mode, with Candidate Configuration mode allowed for the show command only.

csr-gen generates a Certificate Signing Request from user-provided information. The consequence of the command is the creation of a local-certificate in the pending-import state, plus the output of a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then given to an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that import happens, show local-certificate-<id> reports status pending-import, defined as a certificate generated by CSR whose import is not yet complete. Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256, metadata-template to generic, key-usage to digitalSignature,keyAgreement and extended-key-usage to serverAuth,clientAuth. Run from Operational mode. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type defines the requested type of display operation and takes all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details or certificate-hierarchy, with all-certificate-hierarchy as the default. So certificate-hierarchy gives the chain for the named certificate, all-certificate-hierarchy the full hierarchy, and certificate-details only the certificate own contents. certificate is the certificate to display, a string; tab completion lists the installed names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root and trusted-certificate-pace_root, for example display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command shows details of a certificate or CSR and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related local-certificate and peer-certificate objects also expose a trust-chain attribute listing the trusted certificates that constitute the trust chain.

Use the est command, the Enrollment over Secure Transport client, which automates certificate requests, renewals and management over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is the key choice: cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca is the CA set for EST, default 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072 or rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic and also accepts from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client and generic-ikev2-identity. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>], with a matching show. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA. Accepted values are a number of days before expiration, from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the elapsed certificate lifetime, that is of the not-after minus not-before interval rounded up, from 10% to 90% in 10% increments, or disabled. The default is disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned by root-fingerprint, which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection, alongside explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port defaults to 443. Configure with add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], plus set, delete and show forms. server-address is the IP address of the EST server and server-port its port number, default 443. Yes, you can define more than one: each server is keyed by <name>/<server-name> and priority defines the server precedence, range 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence, that is the highest existing number, plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False, default True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base URL, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE directly, from Operational mode. Syntax: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]; import-certificate -h displays help. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. The PEM string carries the certificate(s) and, where applicable, private keys; passphrase decodes encrypted input certificates and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle in addition to the leaf, and for single-certificate files imports intermediates referenced through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. Example: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>.

Check the ISK attributes before clearing. show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], and show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU, true or false, default false. is-key-verified indicates whether the key is verified in this FRU, true or false, default false. being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK; otherwise it is false. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. Remove one with clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where key-name is a string of length 0..64 and must be supplied; -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys (KRKs) and KRK information. Two forms: show KRKs for the whole list, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] for one key, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. name is the unique representation of the object; CPU is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0, a uint8; key-name is the name of the key, a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number is the Key Serial Number; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length is the key length in bits, a uint16; key-payload is the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. It shows the key replacement package (KRP) attributes and is show-only. KRP-version is the package version; key-name is the name of the resource; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), string length 0..20; KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK; signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string 0..1024; signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. install-status indicates whether the KRP has been installed in the system and takes not-installed, installing, installed or failed. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on the local-certificate object: set local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode <value>. It controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked; force-unrevoked forces the opposite. The same set command also accepts alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). id is a unique object identifier for the certificate, a string of length 1..128. Verify with show local-certificate-<id>, which returns revocation-mode along with status, whose values include revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future and valid, plus used-by, the list of secure-applications, ikev2-peers and similar presently using the certificate, and trust-chain and self-signed. The identical revocation-mode attribute, same values and same auto default, exists on peer-certificate. Certificates are deleted with the clear certificate command.

Add the responder with add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], and adjust later with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>]; delete ocsp-server-<name> removes it. priority sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones. Its range is uint8 1..10. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form http://<host>[:<port>], where host is an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional, defaulting to HTTP port 80, for example http://ocsp.example.org; it is a string of length 0..1024. enabled controls whether this OCSP server is consulted for revocation status, true or false, default false, so a new responder must be explicitly enabled. show ocsp-server-<name> returns url, enabled, priority and last-query, the timestamp of the last successful query. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application. Manage it with set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>] and show peer-certificate[-id] with attributes such as version, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, white-listed and revocation-mode. The white-listed flag, true or false with a default of false, means that if true the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain. status values are revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported, with in-use, unused and available deprecated in favour of valid plus the used-by tracking. revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto; alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default allowed.

SSH listens on port 8022 by default, and it is off by default: the enabled attribute, which enables direct access to shell via ssh, is true or false with a default of false. Configure with set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and read it back with show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. port is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell, a number in the range 1..65535, default 8022. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440, with no default. post-login-message is displayed after user login, also a string 0..1440, and defaults to a warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and that the service may be monitored. This object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user; each entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>, which prompts for confirmation. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user, string 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier (name) for this entry, string 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format as <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded OpenSSH public key<SPACE><comment>, a string of 0..2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is read-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. label is a string 0..256.

The node's own SSHv2 host keys are shown with 'show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint]'. These are the global host keys used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 based apps. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, there can be more than one. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. Supported public-key-algorithm values are ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096 and ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts at R9.0). public-key is a PEM-encoded string 0..2048 chars, label 0..256 chars, fingerprint-algorithm is md5 or sha256 and fingerprint is 0..95 chars. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521'.

ssh-keygen generates an SSH private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced by the newly generated pair. Syntax: 'ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]', Operational mode only. -t selects rsa, ecdsa or ed25519; the default type is rsa. -b selects strength: with secure mode (security-policies/secure-mode) disabled, RSA supports 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048) and ECDSA supports 256, 384 or 521 (default 256); with secure mode enabled, RSA supports only 4096 and ECDSA supports 384 or 521 (default 384). ED25519 is 256 regardless of secure mode. -l sets the key label; if omitted the label is the value of ne-id. Retrieve the new public key with 'show ssh-host-key'.

Pre-trust a peer by creating an SSHv2 known-hosts entry: 'add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]'. id is a unique name, string 0..64 chars. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host (an IPv4 or IPv6 address may carry a zone index after a % sign; otherwise the device default zone is used). public-key-algorithm must be one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096 or ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the OpenSSH public key in PEM format, 0..2048 chars; label is 0..256 chars. Use 'set ssh-known-host-<id> [label <value>]' to change the label, 'show ssh-known-host-<id>' to display, and 'delete ssh-known-host-<id>' to remove. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trusted-certificate object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Use 'show trusted-certificate[-id] ...' to view attributes such as version (v3), serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, modification-time, status (in-use, unused, revoked, expired, available, pending-import, invalid, untrusted, future, valid, unsupported), public-key-length (rsa2048/rsa3072/rsa4096/ecdsa256/ecdsa384/ecdsa521), public-key-type (rsa, ecdsa), signature-key-type (rsa, ecdsa, rsassa-pss), signature-hash-algorithm (sha256, sha384, sha512, sha1), certificate-bytes, key-usage and extended-key-usage. Settable attributes are revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default allowed) and label. To remove a certificate use the clear command (clear certificate).

Issue 'terminate cable-id' in Operational mode to stop all running CableID verification tests. Because CableID verification runs on a port-pair basis, the test can only be stopped after the current port-pair verification completes and before the next port-pair starts: the in-flight port-pair runs to completion, so the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once the cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle; after issuing the command use 'show cable-id cable-id-status' to confirm the cable-id entity is back in the idle state. The 'show cable-id' / 'terminate cable-id' pair is documented under the cable-id entity; show is also available in Candidate Configuration mode, terminate only in Operational mode.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM cards; the signal is passed transparently through the OPSM. A CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. Accordingly, cable-id-path card-type-a and card-type-z can only take the values RD20TM or CAD10A, and port-a/port-z are port AIDs on a CableID-capable sled. The card type value is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at that port: when a fiber-connection is created, the CableID function checks whether it terminates on a port of a CableID-capable sled and, if so, records that card type into the CableID path topology as card-type-a or card-type-z. View with 'show cable-id-path-<name>'.

Yes. The cable-id-status container holds the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you may issue 'show cable-id cable-id-status' at any time to query progress. Syntax: 'show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cable-id-state is idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running for the active path only); default idle. test-progress is a string 0..255 chars, default 'None', showing 'Not applicable' if cable-id-state is disabled, otherwise 'N out of M completed' where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number already completed, for example '1 out of 1 completed.'

Each carrier can discover up to one node. carrier-neighbor shows the local carrier instance that has discovered a neighbor node, and it is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. Syntax: 'show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]', in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. local-carrier is a string 0..16 chars; ne-id and ne-name are 0..256 chars; ne-type is 0..64 chars; remote-carrier-id is the AID of the remote carrier (0..64 chars) and implies a specific remote port id. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured.

Use 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. degree-number is a uint16 in range 1..20 and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is a uint32 in range 1..2 and is always 1 in the 1830 GX, since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card, and as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. 'show connection-ports*' lists all connection ports in the node, giving output such as connection-ports-1/1 -> port-1-3-dwdm-line1; 'show connection-ports-5/1' shows the single entry, for example port-name port-4-1-dwdm-line1.

custom-tlv shows the list of Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameters. Syntax: 'show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string 0..64 chars. direction is the direction associated with the LLDP statistics, either ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, a hexadecimal representation of the 24-bit identifier, string 1..6 chars. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV within the scope of that OUI, string 1..507 chars. The value attribute carries the TLV content.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. external-fiber-connection represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Syntax: 'add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]', plus set (label only), show and delete. name is 0..64 chars, node-ids 0..256, card names 0..64, port names 0..128. fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way, default two-way. scope is general-purpose (default) or cable-id; if scope is not cable-id, CableID verification excludes that connection from the CableID path.

fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, used in an OADM/ILA topology: 'add|set fiber-connection-<name> [label] [src-port] [dst-port] [fiber-connection-type]', with show and delete. external-fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and it carries additional attributes: scope (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose), src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name and dst-port-name. The external one is set autonomously by TNMS and manual configuration is not recommended. Both have fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way, default two-way, name 0..64 chars, label 0..256 chars, no pre- or post-conditions.

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol (ICDP, Intelligent Carrier Discovery Protocol) and its global-switch flag defaults to true, so it is enabled by default. Syntax: 'set icdp global-switch <true|false>' and 'show icdp [global-switch]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The global-switch is the flag that enables icdp; permitted values are true and false. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set icdp global-switch true'. The neighbors that ICDP finds are viewed through carrier-neighbor, where each carrier can discover up to one node.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface/Infrastructure. It provides API-based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS. INCI uses a gRPC server/client as the core mechanism: when the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server starts and binds to the local IP address, and when an INCI neighbor instance is configured gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: 'set inci [inci-enabled <true|false>]' and 'show inci [inci-enabled]', with inci-enabled taking true or false and defaulting to false. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Enable with 'set inci inci-enabled true'.

Compare configured-node-name with discovered-node-name on the inci-neighbor. configured-node-name is the user-provisioned name of the remote NE and is explicitly used to compare against the discovered-node-name, which is the name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE; both are strings 0..128 chars. discovered-node-id (string 0..12) carries the node ID received from the remote node. Use 'show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]'. neighbor-id is the node-ID AID of the provisioned neighbor; oper-state is enabled or disabled; alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default inhibited. configured-node-name and neighbor-address are mandatory on add.

Two timers on interface-neighbor control this. discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which SNDP discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered failed; when this timeout occurs the neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. Its range is 300..1800 seconds, default 300. Set them with 'set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. discovery-enabled is true or false, default true, and switches discovery on the local interface. neighbor-adjacency-state can be blackout, discovery, holding or unknown, default unknown. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. The links container within the topology is dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command is simply 'show links', with no command parameters, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The same applies to nct-connection, which shows the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE and is likewise dynamically filled in by the system.

The global lldp object carries the hold-on-timer, which is the time to keep neighbor information in the case where the neighbor does not supply an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. It is a number of seconds and its default is 900. Use 'show lldp [hold-on-timer]' to view the global LLDP configuration and 'set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]' to change it, for example 'set lldp hold-on-timer 60'. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and the lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. On lldp-neighbor, the per-neighbor ttl attribute gives the seconds until the remote system information expires, and if the remote system does not provide a ttl value that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer.

'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]' shows the LLDP local system information sent on an LLDP port. The 1830 GX NE advertises chassis-id-subtype chassis-component with the chassis serial number as chassis-id; port-id-subtype local with the port AID as port-id; port-description set to the port name; system-name set to the NE name; and system-description set to the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> build <software label>'. All these strings are 0..255 chars. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities are router and bridge. Example: 'show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4'.

No. For lldp-neighbor the egress direction is not supported: the direction key is the direction in which the neighbor was detected and its only value is ingress. Syntax: 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-update] [age] [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities] [ttl]', in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics, where direction is ingress only. Example: 'show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress'. The neighbor information is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user.

No. All counter values in an lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. The counters do freeze: all statistical counters associated with a particular port on the local LLDP agent become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. Syntax: 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]'; direction is ingress only, egress is not supported. Counters default to 0, last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z, and total-ageout counts the times a neighbor was deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL expiry.

Use 'show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It shows NCT connectivity information, that is the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE, dynamically filled in by the system so the NCT topology can be derived. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take the values node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned. src-chassis and dst-chassis are the chassis AID if commissioned, or the chassis serial number if unprovisioned (strings 0..64). Likewise src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: the port AID for a commissioned chassis, or the format '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>' for an unprovisioned chassis.

The sndp command sets or shows the SNDP (Simple Neighbor Discovery Protocol) feature switch. Syntax: 'set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]' and 'show sndp [sndp-enabled]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. sndp-enabled is the single attribute, a switch controlling the sndp feature, with values true or false and default true, so SNDP is on unless disabled. Example: 'show sndp sndp-enabled'. SNDP discover messages are the ones sent on management interfaces per the interface-neighbor discovery-cycle-time (30..300 seconds, default 30), with per-interface control through interface-neighbor discovery-enabled.

'add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> [...]' with set, show and delete. The mandatory attributes are src-node-id and dst-node-id (the NE names of the source and destination nodes, 0..256 chars), src-port-name and dst-port-name (the OTS dwdm-line port of the degree, 0..128 chars), and degree-target-tx-power, the launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber. fiber-length defines the fiber length in km of the associated fiber pair, a decimal64 in range 0..25000 km with default 0, and it excludes the length of branch segments. Other attributes: fiber-connection-type two-way (default) or one-way, link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list (0..512), bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0, 0 for end nodes), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition flat-tx or pfib (default pfib), and allocated-spectrum-list of start/end frequency pairs, max 32 elements.

supporting-fiber-connection shows the list of fiber connections supporting a path. Syntax: 'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is the name of the entity, string 0..64 chars, and fiber-connection-list is the supported fiber connection path, an instance-identifier. The same container appears under cable-id-path: it is displayed when the -r flag is used with 'show -r cable-id-path-<name>', which for a single port shows the results from the port-pair including all cable-id-path parameters plus the supporting fiber connections, for example 'supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6' with fiber-connection-list 'supporting-fiber-connection-R1'.

Use `clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>` in Operational Mode. The target is an instance-identifier and may be an lldp-neighbor instance (discovered via LLDP), a carrier-neighbor instance (discovered via ICMP), or an lldp-port-statistics instance (details for an LLDP-enabled port). Example: `clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1`. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Tip: type `clear topology <tab>` to list valid topology objects. To view rather than remove, `show topology` is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode and accepts inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp.

Run `verify [-f] fiber-connection <port-id> [allow-switching]` in Operational Mode; the type-select value fiber-connection is the only verification type supported. If <port-id>/target-select is omitted, all paths are verified. allow-switching is boolean, default false: false verifies active paths only with no system-initiated switching (safe in service); true lets CableID initiate switching on the OPSM so both active and inactive paths are checked. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation (-f skips it), raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE, and is non-blocking; check progress with `show cable-id-status`. Example: `verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true`.

The `bert` command runs in Operational Mode with operations start, stop, get and delete. Start with e.g. `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10`. 100GE/400GE clients use scrambled-idles; ODU4 uses PRBS31 or PRBS31NONINV; CarrierCTP monitoring uses fec-frames. test-signal-direction and test-signal-monitoring-direction are ingress or egress (default none). test-duration is 0 or 10 seconds up to 1000 hours; default 0 means indefinite. Stop with `bert stop test-id=TestX`; test-id is mandatory for stop. If no test-id is given at start, the system generates one. Multiple simultaneous BERTs are allowed on a facility.

The cid-ptp facility is created automatically by the system when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A; managed-by is system, so you cannot create or delete it (only user-created facilities can be user deleted). It represents the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. Only `set` and `show` are supported. On set you can change label (string 0..256); admin-state is not editable and the only supported value is unlock (default unlock), and CableID operation is unaffected by it. Read-only attributes include AID, oper-state (enabled/disabled, default disabled), avail-state, supporting-card/port and `used`, which is true when CableID functionality is supported (default false). Example: `show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid`.

A Digital Coherent 400ZR eth-zr facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type shows 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate is 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable, default ofec, with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7. Degrade monitoring: fdd-monitoring and fed-monitoring are enabled/disabled, both default disabled. Thresholds are decimal64(9) in average BER over range 0.000000001..0.1: fdd-threshold default 0.0195, fdd-clear-threshold default 0.01062, fed-threshold default 0.0206, fed-clear-threshold default 0.01125. link-degrade-indication reports none, local-degraded, remote-degraded or local-and-remote-degraded. Example: `set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000`.

The ethernet facility attribute max-packet-length sets the maximum transfer unit in octets. On 1830 GX G30 the range is 1280..18000 octets; on 1830 GX G40 the range is 1518..18000 octets. The default is 1518 in both cases. It is set with `set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value>` and read with `show ethernet-<name> max-packet-length`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Two restrictions apply: max-packet-length is configurable on card level only and applies to all interfaces on that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs.

`show facilities` lists the facilities configured on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output is a flat list of facility instance names, for example on a 1830 GX G40: super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni, odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1 and odu-1-4-T13. Use it to discover which facility instances exist before addressing them with the per-facility commands.

The `fc` facility (set/show, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode) exposes two Fibre Channel specific attributes for the 32GFC client: `tts`, which enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support (enabled/disabled, default disabled), and `laser-toggling-for-tts`, which enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled (enabled/disabled, default enabled). fc-type is read-only and reports FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G or FC32G. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (default GMP), loopback (none/facility/terminal, default none), loopback-mode, test-signal-type (default none), test-signal-direction (default ingress) and test-signal-monitoring (default false).

The flexo facility reports foic-type read-only, where FOICx.k means k parallel lanes carrying a FlexO-x interface and x is the rate in units of 100G.
