Supported values are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with default foic4.8. fec-type is also read-only: not-applicable, cfec, ofec or noFEC, default ofec. resource-mode is settable and selects ADM (add-drop) or XC (add-drop with regen); the default is ADM. Example: `set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'`. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid (member identity and ordering within a group, need not be sequential) and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds.

`add flexo-group-<name> carriers <value> rate <value> modulation-format <value> group-id <value>` requires four mandatory attributes beyond the name: carriers (a list of carriers bound to the facility, string 1..32), rate (carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s), modulation-format (not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM or BPSK) and group-id (integer 1..1048575, the interface group instance the FlexO-x interface belongs to, unique in the NE). Optional on add are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and fec-type (not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7; default ofec). Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

`high-speed-monitoring` has just two attributes, both set/show in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the user configurable switch that turns high speed monitoring on or off; values true or false, default false. `port` is the user configurable port, a uint16 in the range 1..max, default 57500. Syntax: `set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>]` and `show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]`. It is a singleton container, so no instance name is supplied.

The interlaken facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface and is a system-created facility (managed-by is system only). Its capacity is read-only and fixed at 500 Gbit/s. Settable attributes with `set interlaken-<name>` are label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and loopback (none, facility for a test towards the facility side, terminal for a test towards the terminal side; default none). Read-only show attributes include supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state (enabled/disabled, default disabled) and avail-state. Example: `set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1`.

On line-ptp, auto-in-service is controlled by `auto-in-service-enabled` (true/false, default false) together with `valid-signal-time`, the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal, in the range 1..7200 minutes with a default of 480 minutes. Once a valid signal is detected the facility is automatically brought into service; `remaining-valid-signal-time` (read-only, 1..7200 minutes) shows the actual time left before the auto-in-service mechanism enables the facility. All three are available on add, set and show except remaining-valid-signal-time, which is show only. Example: `show line-ptp-1-2-1` displays auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes, remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes.

They are different commands. `show network-xconnect` is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; it lists the services of multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE. `nw-xconnect` is the provisioning command for an individual networking cross-connection, supporting add, delete, set and show: `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`, `set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>]`, `show nw-xconnect-<name> [AID] [oper-state] [avail-state] [endpoint1] [endpoint2] [xcon-type] [rate]` and `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`. So use network-xconnect to view the list and nw-xconnect to create, modify or delete a specific cross-connection.

Create a user channel cross-connection with `add nw-xconnect-<name> xcon-type <value> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [rate <value>]`. xcon-type values are L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC, default L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0. For a GCC-to-OSC style bridge use L1-ETH-TO-OSC with endpoint1 a comm-eth MO and endpoint2 an OSC-5 comm-channel MO, or L1-OSC-TO-OSC between two OSCX-5 comm-channel MOs; for GCC0 endpoints use a GCC0 comm-channel MO. Both endpoints are mandatory at creation. rate is the maximum bandwidth of the user channel, uint8 range 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. Example: `add nw-xconnect-test1 xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-eth-1-16-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-1-6-dwdm-line-OSCX5`.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created; when a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use `show odu` to determine whether the ODU exists. What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G), that XCONs are mapped into, with `add odu-<name> odu-type <value> [parent-odu <value>] [time-slots <value>] ...`. The pre-condition is that the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added. The read-only `class` attribute distinguishes high-order (the top-most system-created ODUCn/ODUk), low-order (default) and mapped. Example: `add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80`.

Yes. odu-diagnostics instances are addressed as `odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>` where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values. Per direction you can add or set tx-tti, expected-tti, tx-sapi, tx-dapi, tx-operator, expected-sapi, expected-dapi and expected-operator. tti-style selects ITU-T-G709 (TTI split into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, the default) or proprietary (a single 64 byte string). tx-tti and expected-tti are a hex string with 0x prefix of length 1..130 or printable ASCII of length 1..64, default ""; SAPI and DAPI are 1..15 characters (hex 1..32) and operator is 1..32 characters (hex 1..66). Example: `set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPIDAPI-OPER`.

Yes. On the otu facility both fec-mode (the configured FEC mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client) and fec-generation-mode (the FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver) are enabled/disabled with a default of enabled. fec-type defaults to ofec, and the permitted values are not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. All three are available on add, set and show, for example `set otu-<name> fec-mode disabled` or `show otu-<name> fec-mode fec-generation-mode fec-type`. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. otu-type is read-only and reports OTUCn or OTU4.

Set the tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting attribute on otu-diagnostics to SAPI, which reports the TIM alarm on the source access point identifier only rather than the whole trace. The attribute is per direction: `set otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`, direction being ingress or egress. Permitted values are disabled (default, alarm masked), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER and SAPI-DAPI-OPER. Set expected-sapi to the trace you require (hex string with 0x prefix length 1..32 or printable ASCII length 1..15, default "") and keep tti-style at ITU-T-G709 so the TTI is split into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes. Example: `set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`.

The stm facility supports SDH signals STM-16 and STM-64; the read-only stm-type attribute reports which. The name identifies the Synchronous Transport Module N, for example N=16 or 64, per ITU-T G.691. Configure with `set stm-<name>`: label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti (tti-64), loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), test-signal-type (none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31; default none), test-signal-direction (Ingress) and test-signal-monitoring (true/false, default false). Example: `set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP`.

The trib-ptp attribute tributary-disable-action defines what the NE does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). tributary-disable-holdoff-timer delays the client shutdown or replacement signal at egress, uint16 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-shut-off. Related switches are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (enabled/disabled, default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true). Example: `set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off`.

Create a Layer 1 digital cross connect with `add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; source and destination are instance IDs of the end points. direction supports only two-way and defaults to two-way. Example: `add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1`. protection-type is read-only and reports y-cable, snc-n, snc-i or unprotected, with unprotected as the default. Other read-only attributes include type (add, drop, add-drop, express), payload-treatment (transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen, regen-switching), network-mapping and managed-by (user by default; only user created XCONs can be user deleted). `set` allows only label and circuit-id-suffix.

An L2-bridge instance is identified by bridge-name, a string of length 0..64, used as `L2-bridge-<bridge-name>`. Only two attributes are configurable, both with set and show: chassis-name, a leafref to the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. Syntax is `set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>]` and `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]`. Both commands are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Neither attribute has a stated default.

Use `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`, which clears third party apps. The only parameter is app-name, the third party app name. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it, the command prompts. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]` in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. app-name is a leafref to the configured third-party-app app-name. command is one of restart (restarts the third party application), netls (shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers) or exec (executes a third party application operation given in parameters). target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a specific chassis/card AID; it is a string or the value system, and defaults to system. parameters are optional values passed with the command, max 50 elements, applicable when command is restart or exec.

Yes. The call-home command executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server. It forces a connection attempt, and if the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state it forces an immediate attempt rather than waiting before retrying. Syntax: call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>, run in Operational Mode. The single parameter dial-out-server-name is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Pre-condition: the dial-out server must already be configured for the command to execute properly. Examples: call-home dialoutservername, call-home collector-x, and call-home -h for help. This is also how you connect a dial-out-server whose auto-connect is set to false, since such a server can still be connected manually via the call-home RPC.

Use show current-subscription-<subscription-name> with the encoding and transfer-mode attributes (Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode). encoding specifies the data encoding scheme used for data sent to and from the target device, either for all data or optionally per-RPC if the target supports it; permitted values are json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf, with a default of json-ietf. transfer-mode specifies the data transfer mode to the target: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off by the target), or poll (values sent in response to a poll request); the default is stream. Related attributes on the same command include session-protocol (gnmi, default gnmi), session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc) and updates-only (true/false, default false).

No, they are not all loaded by default: the enabled attribute of data-model defaults to false. Use set data-model-<name> enabled true to load a model, and show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled] to view it; show data-model with no name lists all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. enabled allows you to load/unload the data model, and a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces; permitted values are true and false. name is the model name, a string of length 0..256, and description is the data model description, also a string of length 0..256 (show only). Both set and show are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A dial-out-server has a retry-policy attribute with values progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop and retry-forever, defaulting to progressive-back-off. retry is the number of retries and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop; range 0..5, default 3. timeout is the timeout before the next retry, range 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. The port attribute is the dial-out-server session port, range 1..65535, default 4334, which is the default for the netconf protocol over ssh. Configure with add dial-out-server-<name> address <value> [protocol <value>] [port <value>] [retry-policy <value>] [retry <value>] [timeout <value>], or set to change them. Transport is ssh; protocol is netconf or restconf, default netconf.

Yes, gNMI/gRPC is enabled by default: the grpc object's enabled attribute defaults to true, and the port that listens for gNMI access via gRPC defaults to 50051. Use show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity] to view and set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>] to change them, in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. For example, set grpc enabled false disables it. The gnmi-get-encoding-granularity attribute controls the granularity of data in JSON-encoded gNMI Get responses: per-path puts all path data on one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container or list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens on port 830 by default (port-number, uint16, range 1..65535) for NETCONF access via ssh. The hello-timeout attribute specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received or transmitted; a session is dropped if no hello PDU is received or transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. Range is 1..3600 seconds and the default is 2. View and change both with show netconf [enabled] [port] [annotate-cli-name] [static-info-in-notifs] [hello-timeout] and set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [hello-timeout <value>] ..., in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. NETCONF is enabled by default (enabled true), and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session.

Plain HTTP is available but off by default: restconf http-enabled defaults to false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. https-enabled defaults to true. RESTCONF itself is enabled by default (enabled true). The HTTP port (http-port) defaults to 8080 and the HTTPS port (https-port) defaults to 8181, both in the range 1..65535. Session lifetime is governed by cookie-timeout, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, in the range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: set restconf cookie-timeout 10. Use show restconf [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [cookie-timeout] [api-root]; api-root is a read-only string of length 0..64.

Use show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count] in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. snmp-engine-id is the SNMP EngineID of the NE, a string of length 0..256, read-only (show only). It follows the EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC address pool of the NE. engine-boot-count is also show-only and counts how many times the engine has restarted; it is a uint16 with a default of 0. The same object carries the configurable enabled switch for global SNMP access (true/false, default true) and port, the port where the NE listens for SNMP requests (range 1..65535, default 161). Note that trap-community-string lives in the snmp-target object, not here.

No. The community-string-access attribute of snmp-community has read-only as its only permitted value and read-only as its default, so SNMP communities are read-only. Create one with add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>], for example add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true. name is the community name, distinct from the community string itself, a string of length 0..64; community-string is the community string, a string of length 1..32; enabled is the switch to enable or disable this community-string, true or false, default true. set, show and delete snmp-community-<name> are also available, in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The trap-community-string is in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]. snmp-version takes v2c or v3 and defaults to v2c. trap-community-string is the community string used for SNMP traps, a string of length 0..32, default infinera. target-port is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and target-transport is udp (default udp). target-name is a string of 0..32 characters, enabled defaults to true, and snmpv3-user only applies when snmp-version is v3. Example: add snmp-target-mytarget snmp-version v2c target-ip 10.220.225.10 target-port 162 target-transport udp trap-community-string public enabled true. set, show and delete are also supported.

A new SNMPv3 user defaults to user-sec-level no-auth-no-priv; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy algorithms available in priv-protocol are DES, AES128, AES192 and AES256, with AES128 as the default. auth-protocol supports only SHA (default SHA). Create a user with add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]; auth-passphrase and priv-passphrase are mandatory and are strings of length 8..64, and the user name is a string of length 1..32. Example: add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123. set, show and delete are also available.

The subscription-path-mode attribute of subscription-path controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change or sample, with target-defined as the default. sample-interval is the time in milliseconds between the device's samples of a telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription, if sample-interval is not set the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. heartbeat-interval is the maximum time in milliseconds that may pass between updates, default 0; for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset and heartbeat-interval below 10 seconds, the system adjusts heartbeat-interval to 20 seconds. suppress-redundant (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates. View with show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>.

Use show subscriptions. It shows a list of subscriptions and takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For more detail on the individual telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use show current-subscription-<subscription-name> with attributes such as related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the paths within a subscription, use show subscription-path or show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> with attributes subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode, sample-interval, heartbeat-interval and suppress-redundant.

Telemetry is configured through the telemetry object. The command is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry, and the object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Syntax: show telemetry to view it and set telemetry id <string> to configure it, in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The single parameter is id, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, a string of length 0..4096 with no default. Example: show telemetry. The guide does not draw a further distinction between persistent and dynamic beyond that description; the related views of the resulting subscriptions are show subscriptions, show current-subscription-<subscription-name> and show subscription-path.

Use show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable], or show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]. The state attribute reports the third party app state with values running, stopped or failed, defaulting to stopped. It is not enabled by default: the enable attribute defaults to false. enable is the third-party-app enabled state, true or false; if enabled the app is started, and the app is also enabled upon system restart, and if disabled the app is stopped. Set with set third-party-app-<app-name> [version <value>] [vendor <value>] [product <value>] [label <value>] [state <value>] [information <value>] [enable <value>]. version is a string 0..64, vendor 0..64, product 0..256, information 0..1024. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the add command, which creates a new managed entity in the system database. Type add <tab> to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time; the guide also lists the creatable entities, including aaa-server, access-rule, ace, acl, card, chassis, dial-out-server, dns-server, file-server, interface, ipv4-address, ipv4-static-route, log-server, ntp-server, snmp-community, snmp-target, snmpv3-user, task, template, tom, user, user-group and xcon. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided on creation; if a mandatory attribute is not given in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Syntax: add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]. -v validates only, -m merges (best effort add), -f forces without confirmation. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add.

Yes, by default. In all cases the clear command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided; -f forces the command without confirmation. Syntax is clear -h or clear [-f] <subcommand> ..., and the command runs in Operational Mode. Subcommands include alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology. For example, clear -f pm ... or clear -f system type=... will skip the prompt. Note that clear system factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards. Similar force behaviour exists on delete, default, add and exit via their own -f flags.

Yes, with the show-alarm-columns attribute of the cli object, which sets the columns to display in the output of the show alarm CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, default-columns to show the pre-defined columns, or default-columns,<additional-details> to show the additional-details column alongside the pre-defined ones. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3, and set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action to add the corrective-action column as the last column. Use show cli to view it. The same object also carries enabled (default true), port (range 1..65535, default 22), script-dir and default-interactive-mode (default true).

Use set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes display. Range is 10..1000 with a default of 40. The companion cli-columns sets the number of columns for display, range 80..4000, default 80. For example: set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30 and set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-columns 100. View with show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]. The same object also holds interactive-mode (true/false, default true, set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes. The connect command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI. Syntax: connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>], available in Operational Mode. target-address is a mandatory attribute and may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or a hostname if DNS is configured; it requires connectivity. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional, defaulting to 22, but can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Example: connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022, which then adds the host to the known hosts list and prompts for the password of admin@10.41.24.55.

Yes, use convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. target-representation may be netconf-xml (a full NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (the same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted, snmp-oids (OIDs for the objects in a show command) or netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing an SNMP request). The command string should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by semicolons are merged into a single payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered.

No. The default command assigns default values to the targeted entities, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes that are only settable at creation. If you specify attributes, only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Syntax: default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*], with -f forcing the command without confirmation and -h showing help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: default user-peter, default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/EQPTMSMT, default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*, default alarm-severity-entry-*, and default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: delete -b <object> is the best effort delete introduced in R9.0. It bypasses the check for object existence without returning a failure, so it does not fail if the object does not exist, whereas the standard delete <object> does fail in that case. delete -b has the same functionality as a NETCONF remove operation. Note that -b does not raise an error if the object is missing but may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures. Full syntax: delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]. For scripting you will usually also want -f, which forces the command without confirmation, since delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt; -v validates only and replies with OK if valid. Deleting an entity removes it and all its sub-level objects.

The exit command logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in Operational Mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in Candidate Configuration Mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided. Syntax: exit [-h|-f], where -h displays help for the command and -f forces the command without confirmation. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as exit -f, so it leaves the mode or ends the session immediately with no confirmation prompt. Example: exit -f.

Use the expect command, which ensures that an attribute matches an expected value. Syntax: expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes; wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. If the script runs in stop-on-error mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123 and expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*

Yes, use the export command. Syntax: export [-h] and export [<variable>=[<value>]]. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Variables are referenced with ${variable} in any CLI command, which is particularly useful in CLI scripts. Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed; they do not survive logout. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. 'export SLOT_NUMBER=2' declares a variable, 'export SLOT_NUMBER=' deletes it, and a bare 'export' lists all existing variables, for example: export MYSESSIONID='10.100.152.29:56154' and export MYUSERNAME='admin'.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from within the CLI in Operational mode, and both accept a single command to execute instead of an interactive shell; exiting returns to the CLI prompt. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' launches the shell on the node itself, using the currently logged in user, allowing only commands accessible to that user; user access to shell can be limited to the NA, NE and TT user-groups, and specific scripts can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted binaries include /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). 'gshell [-h] [<cmd>]' instead launches the bash shell inside a Guest Container, and has the pre-condition that the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Examples: 'shell ifconfig', 'gshell ls -l'.

No. kill-session <session-id> closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), but the <session-id> must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and it cannot match the id of the current session. To end your own session use the normal 'exit' command instead. Use 'show session' to display the list of current sessions and their ids before killing one. Access mode is Operational mode. The session-id parameter is a string with no default. Example: kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212.

Use the message command, which sends a message to other CLI sessions. Syntax: message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]. Access mode is Operational mode. message content is a string of 1-4096 characters. target defaults to 'all', so by default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions; other target values are 'local' (only local sessions, serial console or CRAFT), 'remote' (only remote sessions, for example SSH), a specific session-id, or a username (all CLI sessions of that user). The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions. Example: message 'System will reboot in 5 minutes', or to one session: message 'System reboot in 5 minutes' 0.0.0.0:36.

Properties are type-specific, auto instantiated by the system but configurable by the user. Syntax: 'show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]' and 'set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]'. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Two property-name values are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures, with values disabled or enabled and default disabled; and max-packet-length, which indicates the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO, with a range of 1518 to 18000 and default 1518. Example: set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled.

Use the run command, which executes a previously configured/defined/scheduled task or a script. Syntax: 'run task [[task-name=]<value>]' and 'run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]'. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, with the pre-condition that the task or script to be called must be defined. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name. script-name is a relative path to the script directory, and arguments are optional. Flags: -q executes the script in quiet mode (only command output is shown, otherwise both the command and its output are shown), -r runs the script as a declarative config script that replaces system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop, or rollback. Examples: run task collect-diag; run script config.cli -e=stop -q.

Both are add/set/show/delete commands for individual user-configurable scheduled commands, and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. They address the same scheduled-tasks container: the scheduled-task form is 'add/set/delete scheduled-task-<name>' with 'show scheduled-tasks' listing the container of all entries, while the task form is 'add/set/show/delete task-<name>' for the individual scheduled task, and 'run task <task-name>' resolves against /ne/system/scheduled-tasks/task/name. The task page documents the fuller attribute set: name (0..64 chars), enabled (true/false, default true), label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), command (1..1024), command-type (cli), frequency, number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit), start-time, end-time (default never), persistent (default true), plus the read-only task-status (scheduled, disabled, finished, ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output.

Only if you are an SA user. 'show session' lists currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; remaining users can only see their own session. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if the session is initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI when using Cookie Based Authentication; the session keep-alive is 5 minutes by default and is changed with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. The set command can set an attribute on multiple instances simultaneously using the wildcard (*): as a replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), as a replacement of a single instance key (port-1-4-*; port-1-*-3), as a replacement of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*; ethernet-*), and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). Square brackets represent ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]; trib-ptp-[1-4-T1,1-6-T16,1-7-T15]). One or more filters of the form <attribute>=<value> can also restrict the set to matching entities, for example 'set port port-type=line admin-state lock'. All attribute-value pairs must belong to the same managed entity. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or when it implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates. Example: set port-1-4* admin-state lock.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. The command runs in Operational mode, syntax 'shell [-h] [shell command]'. The shell is launched using the currently logged in user and allows the commands accessible to that user, so Linux-side permissions still apply. The Linux shell is closed the normal way (for example with 'exit'), returning to the CLI prompt, and a single shell command can also be executed inline. Certain commands and scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing them with 'sudo'; the permitted set includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts such as download.sh, install_os.sh, config_ip.sh, config_dns.sh, tunnelctl.sh, docker.sh and CopyLogsToUSB.sh.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request rather than dumping everything: give an individual <entity-id> or a generic <entity-type>, add filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, name specific attributes, or limit recursion with -r=<n> (n levels down; full recursion if n is omitted). Other flags that reduce output are -c (container instances only, no attributes), -a (attributes only, no container instances), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) and -o (state/read-only attributes only). For long but permitted output, pipe through '| more' to page it, since the page size matches the CLI session window. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the simulate command, which triggers simulated events in the system (alarms, equipment, etc). Access mode is Operational mode. Syntax: simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>]). trigger values are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru; note that plug-out-fru is not supported. For equipment simulation you provide the holder-AID (string 1..64, matching the card slot or the tom port); for plug-in the card/tom type is required and subtype is optional. For alarms, alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto (selected by the system), and if alarmed-entity or alarm-type is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. The command works on a simulator and on a real system, but on a real system the simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real hardware, for example you cannot simulate plugout of hardware that is physically present. Example: simulate plug-in-fru 1-5.

Yes. The sleep command specifies a delay for a specified amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. Syntax: 'sleep -h' or 'sleep <time in seconds>'. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The single parameter is the duration of the delay in seconds. 'sleep 1' pauses one second and 'sleep 0.1' pauses 100 milliseconds. The -h flag displays help for the command.

Add a task with a start-time and no frequency: an empty frequency means a single-occurrence task. For example: add task-db_backup_once command 'upload database file-server=xfr1' start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label 'DB Backup once'. This requires that the file server xfr1 be configured before the command is used. Full syntax: add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is up to 64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, command-type defaults to cli, enabled defaults to true, persistent defaults to true (the task survives a system restart), end-time defaults to never. After it has run, 'show task-<name>' reports task-status finished, plus previous-run, previous-result (success or fail) and previous-output.

The terminate command stops a running operation, in Operational mode. Forms: 'terminate location-led <entity>' stops a location led test previously started with activate, where the entity is a chassis or a card (no effect if no test is active); 'terminate otdr [entity=]<value>' stops an ongoing OTDR measurement for the given port; 'terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>' stops a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, aborting the scan abruptly, restoring otdr ne function attributes, keeping logs and available OTDR result files, and reverting ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state (if it was fail, the PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED alarm is raised again); 'terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*' terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated; 'terminate cable-id' stops the CableID verification test. CableID verification stops only after the current port-pair test completes, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time; confirm it with 'show cable-id cable-id-status' and look for cable-id-state changing to idle.

update triggers a system-driven re-evaluation of specific object attributes selected by <type>, rather than assigning an operator-supplied value the way set does. Syntax: update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*], and multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Access mode is Operational mode only (set also works in Candidate Configuration mode). The supported type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the under commissioning state; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the Ready for Service state. The last two apply to NE entities in SLTE systems. Examples: update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line; update filter-insertion-date-now chassis.

Use the tic and toc auxiliary commands. tic starts a timer for the typed command and toc displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Wrap the command you want measured between them on one line, separated by semicolons: 'tic;show log;toc'. The same works for a list of commands in a script: 'tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc', which reports the elapsed time for the whole sequence.

Yes. Use 'help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]', which searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be provided using a wild card, for example 'help -s inventory' or 'help -s data*'. Related help forms: '?' alone displays the list of all available commands; 'help <command/container/attribute>' displays information on how that command, container or attribute can be used (for example 'help show'); '<command> ?' displays the possible addressable parameters (show ?); '<command> -?' displays the possible options (show -?); '<command> -h' displays the complete help (show -h); '<command> <container> ?' displays the hierarchy sub-containers and attribute list of the container; and '<command> <attribute> ?' displays the list of attributes of the container. Both help commands are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so an alias you define stays after you log out and is visible to other operators. The alias command defines a more user-friendly alphanumeric string for one or more commands, containers, attributes or values. Syntax: 'alias [-h]' and 'alias [<name>=<value>]'. Access mode is Operational mode. alias with no arguments prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Quotes must be used for multi word values, aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by using quotes. Aliases are removed with the unalias command. Examples: 'alias s=show' and 'alias sa='show alarm''.

Run 'unalias -a', which removes all alias definitions. Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, since aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so clearing them affects every operator on the node, not just you. Syntax: 'unalias -h', 'unalias -a', 'unalias [<name> ...]'. Access mode is Operational Mode. To remove specific ones, name them: 'unalias foo' or 'unalias bar baz qux'. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Aliases are added and visualized with the alias command.

Use the tree flags. 'tree -d=depth' sets the maximum display depth of the tree, where depth is the number of levels to display; if not specified, all levels are displayed by default, up to max depth from the current working entity or the provided entity id. 'tree -a <entity id>' displays the entity ancestors only, that is just the target entity and all its ancestors, for example 'tree -a interface-DCN'. Full syntax: 'tree [-h]' and 'tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])'; -o displays a tree based on a YANG top node. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The tree shows only managed entities including all existing instances, with no attribute names or values, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with '| more', for example 'tree | more', or 'tree -d=2' for two levels from the current scope.

edit navigates the managed entity hierarchy to any entity: 'edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]', with absolute IDs starting from the root of the system or relative to the current entity shown in the path banner, for example 'edit card-1-1' or the relative form 'edit chassis-1 slot-2'. Editing a nonexistent entity instance fails. up brings the current path up by one path level, changing the currently selected entity to its parent; it takes no parameters and has no impact at the hierarchy top level. top brings the current path directly to the top of the managed entity hierarchy [ne]. All three run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and the effect of each is visible on the CLI banner, for example [ chassis-1 ] after 'edit chassis-1' and [ ne ] after 'top'.

Use the history command, which displays the current session's command history as a numbered list. Each command can be repeated using '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and '!!' repeats the previous command. Syntax: 'history [-h]'. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; the command takes no parameters other than -h. To search for particular entries, filter with piped commands, for example: history | include 'show'.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level the up command has no impact. up brings the current path up by one path level in the managed entity hierarchy, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent level, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner. Once the banner shows [ ne ], further up commands leave you there. Syntax is 'up [-h]'; the command does not support any parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands are edit, which navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and top, which navigates to the top of the hierarchy root. Example progression: edit card-1-5 gives [ card-1-5 ], up gives [ equipment ], up again gives [ ne ].

grep and include do the same job: each is a piped command called against the result of a previous command, and each displays only the lines matching <filter>. The guide states explicitly that grep is the same as the include command. Both accept multiple words separated by spaces when enclosed in quotes, both support regex, both do a case insensitive comparison (show | grep abc equals show | grep ABC), and both can be chained with other piped commands. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> shows n lines of context after the actual match, -b=<n> shows n lines of context before the actual match, and -n displays line numbers in the result. include has no such options, only -h and <filter>. The complementary filter is exclude, which drops matching lines.

Yes. Use the `display` piped command with the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configurations as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and is specifically useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. To capture the whole node configuration, run `show -r | display commands`. The other supported `display` modes are: list (the default display mode, one value per line), table (rows are instances, columns are attributes), csv (comma separated values, useful for pasting into a spreadsheet), keys-table (like table but instance representation split per individual keys), single-table (like table but merges all tables into one, useful when retrieving the same data in multiple entities), only-values (only the value of the requested attributes, useful for script building), xml (similar to NETCONF responses), json (similar to RESTCONF response), xpath, and interactive (JSON in the 'jless' interactive viewer; 'q' or CTRL-C to leave, ':help' for help). `display -h` shows help.

Yes. Pair the `begin` and `until` piped commands: `begin` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, with the output beginning at the line that matches the word; `until` displays the output ending at a specified word, with the output ending at the line that matches the word. The guide states explicitly that `begin` can be used together with the `until` piped command to retrieve a sub-set of an output (and vice versa). Syntax is `<command> | begin <words>` and `<command> | until <words>`; `<words>` is the line to begin with / end with, and it may contain spaces if in quotes. Both accept `-h` to display help. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command line, so the two can be chained on one command.

Yes, and the position matters. The `more` piped command displays long outputs incrementally, page by page: `<command> | more [-h]`. Multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, i.e. it is tied to the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display is paused; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> and <tab>) shows the next page. Example of pairing it with a filter: `tree | include led | more`. Also `show -r | more`.

It does not fail. With the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used, it will be ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`, where `<attribute>` is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output; `sort -h` displays help. To flip the order, use `-i`, which inverts the order in the output and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. `sort` with no parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. Examples: `show card | sort` (same as `show card` alone), `show port | sort port-type`, `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date` (sorted by user-group then last-login-date, inverted), and `show odu | sort -i`.

Capitalisation does not matter, and yes, patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out the lines containing a defined word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>`. The `<filter>` does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed in quotes. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. `exclude -h` displays help. Examples: `show | exclude ne`, `show | exclude 'ne oper'`, and `show led | exclude status`. The inverse commands are `include` (displays only lines that include the filtering text) and `grep` (the same as `include`); both are likewise case insensitive and regex-capable.

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`. More than one word can be provided. The distinction is quoting: words given without quotes are searched for separately, while words enclosed in quotes are searched for as a sentence, i.e. the whole phrase. So `<word>` is any word to highlight and may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. `highlight -h` displays help. Examples: `show odu | highlight odu4` highlights one word; `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` highlights the two words 'odu4' and 'oduflex' separately; and `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the word 'odu4'.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, with `<command>` being any display command such as `tree` or `show`; `<command> | linenum -h` displays help for the command. It takes no other parameters. Example: `show | linenum` displays the output with enumerated lines. If you want line numbers only on filtered results, the `grep` piped command has an equivalent option: `-n` displays line numbers in the result, alongside `-a=<n>` (number of lines of context to show after the actual match) and `-b=<n>` (number of lines of context to show before the actual match), used as `<command> | grep [<option>] <filter>`.
